speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, March 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. E. W. George for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Fair, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Bryce.

maintopic: SPEECH FROM THE THRONE
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak today on the question of double taxation and its evil results, more particularly with regard to its effect on home ownership. I propose particularly to deal with municipal taxation and the cost of education, and I shall endeavour to show that under present taxation arrangements the householder is being discriminated against and penalized to such an extent that his security of tenure is being threatened.
In a previous session the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) recognized the basic evil of double taxation and brought in an amendment to the Income Tax Act whereby owners of Canadian stocks and other equities could deduct 10 per cent of their income from such sources when computing their taxable income. This was a wise provision, although it could hardly be considered generous. My submission is that if it is just and right to admit the evils of double corporation taxation, surely it is even more just and right to admit the principle with regard to municipal taxation.
In Canada today I believe double taxation reaches a greater intensity than it does in any other country in the world. We have a corporation tax, including the provincial impost, of some 54 per cent. On top of this there is personal income tax, which rapidly

rises to 30 per cent on a comparatively small income, and then proceeds in the higher brackets actually to take more in taxes than is received in income. To this is added the universal sales tax of 10 per cent, and on many items an excise tax of 25 per cent as well. Added to this are the direct provincial levies, and finally municipal taxation.
In the calculation of the tax liability in each case no consideration is given to the taxpayer for what he has paid in other forms of taxation. Thus you compound the tax liability and, as I hope to show, this is as great an evil as compounding a felony. The impact of this system is felt most heavily by the middle class, who, for want of a better definition, I shall describe as all those who own or are in the process of purchasing a home, and whose financial status is such that this constitutes their principal capital investment.
While I realize that municipal taxation is not directly a federal matter, nor are educational costs, nevertheless their crippling effect is undermining the security of such a large segment of the Canadian people that this House of Commons can no longer stand aloof.
In what I have to say, Mr. Speaker, I shull ask for no grants and no expenditure of money by the federal government for municipal taxation, but I will ask that the impact of certain measures of double taxation be done away with. The difference between municipal taxation and income taxation is this: income taxation is based1 on the general principle of the ability to pay, whereas municipal taxation is based on value, sometimes an arbitrary value, set on the taxpayer's home and property, and levied against him frequently, and I might say generally, without his having an opportunity to do very much about the taxation so levied.
In the depression of the 1930's the destruction of property values through the increase of municipal costs was one of the most serious results of that grave time. My reason for speaking today, Mr. Speaker, is that there is throughout Canada an incipient condition which could easily lead to the same thing that happened in the 1930's. We have today municipality after municipality complaining about the added1 cost of direct relief. We have, as I hope to show in a minute, rapidly increasing taxation on real property, and there is a growing apprehension amongst municipal bodies about what the future holds for them. Here I want to say that there is no segment of the Canadian people, or of the people of any democracy, who need to be protected as does the middle class. They are the people who pay the bulk of the taxes, do the fighting
The Address-Mr. Adamson when there is a war, and do the great majority of the work. They are the very backbone of the country. As a matter of fact, the destruction of the middle class is inevitably the step which is taken either deliberately or accidentally before a dictatorship seizes any country.
Few people have built up sufficient capital by way of common stocks or other equities to provide for their financial security. The security of the huge majority of the mass of Canadians is in their own homes and property. To jeopardize these is to strike a blow at the very foundations of our society. This is recognized by a group of people who should know-and I am referring to the Canadian federation of mayors and reeves of municipalities-who stated that the problems they face are these:
1.	The costs of municipal services are fast outstripping the limited revenue sources available to municipal governments.
2.	The present municipal tax structure is too rigid or too limited to serve as an adequate base upon which the, financial affairs of local governments can continue to be carried on effectively.
What do they mean by that? They mean that their sources of revenue are fixed. They are directly fixed upon real estate and homes, which are the only taxable assets in a municipality. While I believe it would be unthinkable to enlarge the scope of municipal taxation, I make that statement as a personal observation, there must be some way in which this burden of necessary costs of the municipalities can be more equitably spread across the whole financial structure of the country.
The tax demands of municipalities is having a punitive effect in many constituencies in Canada, particularly in those constituencies where, through shifts of population and increased industrialization as in many of our eastern metropolitan areas, rapid growth has taken place. My own constituency, for which I speak, is a case in point. In the constituency of York West, which I have the very great honour of representing, there are two townships. The first of these, part of the township of York, has a population of nearly 100,000, while in the township of Etobicoke there is at present a population of between 55,000 and 60,000. In both these townships, particularly in Etobicoke, there has been a rapid increase since the taking of the census. York West contains, as well, five other smaller municipalities of between 10,000 and 15,000 each. Therefore municipal problems of metropolitan and suburban corporations are of vital interest to my constituents.
I propose therefore to show the house what real estate taxation means to my constituents, and with your indulgence I shall endeavour

ordinary householder. To do this I have taken three different types of dwelling, namely, the small house, the medium house, and the large or expensive house.
In the case of a small house the 1949 taxes amounted to $47; in 1952 I estimate they will total $66, an increase of 58 per cent. The interesting thing about it is that the educational taxes increased from $16 to $32, an increase of 100 per cent. In the case of a medium house the taxes increased from $143 to $197, or 38 per cent, in the same period, but for educational purposes they have increased by 93 per cent. In the case of a large house, the 1949 taxes were $765 as compared with an interpolated $1,182 in 1952, an increase of 54 per cent, but for educational purposes the taxes increased from $263 to $593, an increase of 126 per cent.
This shows how the cost of running municipalities has seriously accelerated in the last three or four years. If it continues, the man who owns his own house will see his equity decreased by municipal taxation, because it is like a perpetual mortgage which increases year by year but which can never be paid off.

I have spoken to people from Ottawa and elsewhere and I gather that the pattern is similar all across Canada. I have the figures for Canada, but as they have been published elsewhere I shall not burden the house with them. Suffice to say that they show a similar picture, although perhaps not quite as intense in its over-all effect as is shown by metropolitan municipalities like Etobicoke and York. The burden is becoming so intolerable that the wisdom of owning a home is becoming questionable.
With reference to the regulations in effect in the United States I asked the National House Builders Association Incorporated of the city of Toronto to provide me with some comparisons of building costs and taxation as between the United States and Canada. I will not read the whole of this letter, which is signed by Angus Gordon, secretary of that association, but I should like to read one or two paragraphs:
Attached are excerpts from replies to queries from this association to the United States treasury department. As you will see, real estate receives consideration both in the matter of mortgage interest payments and municipal taxation.
Then further on:
However, in conversation with Mr. Harry Barrington, president of the Salt Lake City home builders association and Mr. Alan Brockbank, president of the national association of home builders of the United States, X was informed that they are able to construct homes costing $10,000
14, 1952
The Address-Mr. Adamson and under in Utah with a down payment of $1,200 and carrying charges including taxation which bring monthly payments to as low as $48 over a thirty years amortization period.
Then he says:
This compares much too unfavourably with our own general picture. For a $10,000 home the average down payment throughout Canada would amount to $3,000, while to qualify a worker would have to be in receipt of at least $3,200 per annum.
In speaking about municipal taxation he refers to my own constituency and says:
You will realize in your own municipality of Etobicoke that school costs are stifling the men who are attempting to develop properties in the area. While nothing official has been issued, builders know that they have to add at least $1,000 per lot to the cost for the provision of school buildings before they can take up permits for the area.
He goes on to talk about the necessity for town planning and restrictions on speculative sales of real estate. I also have here the statement of the United States income tax department, signed by the deputy commissioner of the branch, setting forth that income tax policy in the United States is to allow both mortgage interest and municipal taxation as deductions from income for taxation purposes.
Before proceeding with the suggestions I have to offer I should like to mention briefly the matter of education. Today very serious questions are being raised all across both Canada and the United States with respect to the effectiveness of our educational system. Just the other day at the convocation of the university of Toronto Dr. Hutchins, of the university of Chicago, stated that it was entirely possible for a man to graduate from a university in the United States without being able to read or write. He was too polite, of course, to say anything about the Canadian system of education; but Dr. Sidney Smith, head of the university of Toronto, has had some pretty devastating things to say about the failure of first year students at that university. Many articles have been written, including one quite recently in Maclean's magazine by a noted educationist, calling into question the effectiveness of the Canadian educational system.
I realize that this is in no way a federal matter at the present time; but with the mounting costs, with the federal government having made grants to universities, with the critical situation facing the municipalities, with the criticism being raised on every hand about our educational system, is it likely that we in this house can completely neglect and stand aloof from this problem? I do not believe it is. I am convinced that with the present high taxation and with the tremendous percentage of the national income that is being spent by the federal

The Address-Mr. Howe authority, this house must take into consideration the welfare of the municipalities. We cannot allow that branch of government which is closest to the people to become unable to function through inability to meet its responsibilities. If we neglect this essential part of our governmental system in Canada we destroy a vital part of the democratic process.
I wish to offer the Minister of Finance the following proposals:
1.	That all municipal taxation be allowed as a deduction from income for taxation purposes.
2.	That personal expenditures on education for one's own family be allowed as a deduction, irrespective of the age of the student, thus assisting technical and medical students.
3.	That mortgage interest payments on the dwelling lived in by the taxpayer be allowed as a similar deduction. This should be allowed in the same way and for the same reasons that citizens are allowed to deduct interest paid on stocks or bonds which are in the process of being bought.
4.	The calling of a conference of all provincial ministers of education with the Minister of Finance or his or their deputies to explore means of providing direct aid to education; the conference also to consider the possibility of a national program on education so that students moving from one province to another would not find such a discrepancy between various provincial jurisdictions.
This problem is as vital as almost any we face today. Security, Mr. Speaker, starts with the family. To continue the trend which I have tried to outline today, of allowing ever-increasing taxation to jeopardize the security of the home, strikes at the very vitals of our democratic system.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: SPEECH FROM THE THRONE
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with previous speakers in congratulating the mover (Mr. George) and seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address. Both acquitted themselves splendidly, and both demonstrated their ability to take an effective part in the work of parliament.
It has been my custom to at this time give a progress report of the work of the departments for which I am responsible, and I propose to follow that custom today. I shall not attempt to give a statistical review, but rather to cover the general situation as it appears now. Just about a year ago Canada got started on a three-year defence program.


Speaking at that time I outlined what the government was doing to set the defence production part of that program in motion, and what the effect was likely to be on the economy of the country. Today, one year later, I can report substantial and, on the whole, satisfactory progress. I can report also that the basic decision then taken to keep government controls to the minimum and as flexible as possible has proved to be the right decision. In the light of what has happened, it is fortunate that the government did not accept the advice of those on the opposition side of the house who at that time thought an extensive system of direct controls should be adopted forthwith.
I cannot think of a better way of summarizing the position than to say that we are taking the defence preparations in our stride. The expectation of acute shortages and of serious dislocations in the civilian sector arising from these defence preparations have not been realized. As has happened on many occasions in the past, the Canadian economy has shown once again that it is capable of a remarkable response to demands for adjustment and for greater output. I do not believe that these reserves of economic potential are by any means exhausted.
In saying this I do not mean to suggest that we can now relax, and that our defence objectives can be attained without effort or sacrifice. Far from it. The greater part of the job as presently planned is still to be done, and no one can be at all sure that we shall not be faced with new emergencies calling for even greater efforts. Events of the past year should have demonstrated, however, that Canada can play a full and honourable part in the strengthening of the free world against the threat of aggression and still retain a free, progressive and reasonably stable economy.
The first year of the defence program is drawing to a dose. Hon. members will, I think, be interested in the answers to two questions. First, have the objectives been attained? What is there to show for the moneys and effort expended? There will be many opportunities during this session to examine into the progress of the defence program. My purpose at this time is to give a brief and broad outline of what has been happening to that part of the program for which the Department of Defence Production is responsible. Hon. members will recall that approximately $1,700 million was appropriated for defence purposes during the current fiscal year, or about one-third of the three-year $5 billion program then contemplated. Of this $1,700 million, about.

$1,100 million was earmarked for expenditure on military equipment and installations. We shall not spend the full amount during the current fiscal year. How much less is uncertain, but if defence production progress continues at the current rate there will remain at the end of the fiscal year a sum of $200 million, more or less, unspent toy the Department of Defence Production.
I shall discuss the reasons for that shortfall in expenditure, but before doing so it may be worth emphasizing at the outset that it is not the result of a deliberate slow-down in the pace of preparedness. We set out to try to complete and pay for one-third of the three-year program in one year. That was an ambitious undertaking, perhaps too ambitious considering the specialized nature of the Canadian program, and the resulting need for extensive preparation and tooling-up before the production stage could be reached. The sights were set high deliberately so that there would be continuing pressure to do better; that pressure has never been relaxed. While there have been changes in the content of the program, and while some production schedules have experienced delays running as long as several months, I have every reason to believe that within the three-year period we shall do in physical terms, in terms of construction put in place and quantities of supplies and equipment produced and delivered, what we set out to do and probably somewhat more, for we have taken on additional commitments in the meantime.
There are a number of reasons why we shall not spend quite as much as was appropriated in the current fiscal year. There is no single cause, and indeed it is difficult to assess the effects of the different causes. One, of course, is the delays experienced in the procurement of equipment that was to be purchased outside of Canada. I am not blaming other countries for those delays. They have encountered much the same problems we have. Another is the fact that we were unable to get an important section of our weapons and ammunition program under way until recently because specifications had not been received. Then, you will probably have heard a great deal about the shortage of machine tools in the United States. Mr. Charles E. Wilson, head of the mobilization effort in that country, in his fourth quarterly report to the president dated January 1 of this year, said:
Despite everything that has been or can be done to increase production, machine tools will remain the most important factor limiting military production for many months to come.
The Address-Mr. Howe
That shortage has had a direct effect on the progress of defence preparations here in Canada. In spite of the growth of our own machine tools industry, Canada continues to depend heavily on imports from across the line.
Looking back, knowing what could not be known a year ago, it is easy to show-and I have no hesitation in saying-that there are some things which should have been done differently. That is the advantage of hindsight. On the whole, however, I submit that the program for which the Department of Defence Production is responsible is away to an excellent start. This first year has been used to good advantage. May I repeat the words used by the Prime Minister when speaking in this debate. Although the job done during this first year "may not be ideal and may not be as good as any of us would hope it could or should be, I think we have to be realistic enough to realize that it is as good as can be done under existing circumstances".
It was essentially a year of making ready. It was a year devoted in large measure to designing and engineering, to tooling-up, to organizing and recruiting, to testing and modifying-preliminary tasks which must be undertaken and accomplished before the production lines can roll. In many respects this stage of preparation is even more important under present circumstances than the later stage of production, for our aim is not to produce the maximum number of aircraft or electronic equipment, or ships, or guns as quickly as possible. Rather it is to produce in the next few years enough of these instruments of warfare to bring our defences and the defences of our allies up to what is considered to be an adequate level, and to be ready in the event of all-out war to produce at full blast.
As I have already indicated, the Department of Defence Production will probably spend about $900 million more or less during the present fiscal year. Until the results for the month of March are in, I cannot give a detailed breakdown of these expenditures for the year. Roughly speaking, however, about three-quarters represents expenditure in Canada and one-quarter expenditure in the United States. Half of the purchases from the United States will be for aircraft, engines and parts.
Now let me break the figures down by what we in the department refer to as programs. On previous occasions I have pointed out that, over the whole three-year period,
438	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Howe the Department of Defence Production plans to spend about one-third of the moneys appropriated by parliament on aircraft. As nearly as can be estimated, about the same proportion-that is, one-third-of the present year's expenditures will be on the aircraft program. Construction of military installations accounts for about 17 per cent; clothing and textiles about 8 per cent; electronics about 6 per cent; shipbuilding about 6 per cent; tanks, mechanical transport, weapons, ammunition and explosives produced in Canada, among them, another 10 per cent; purchases from the United States for the first and second divisions about 5 per cent; and the remainder, 15 per cent.
This is money spent or to be spent within the current fiscal year. It is money spent in payment for deliveries, in payment for construction put in place, and as progress payments for development and pre-production expenses.
Orders have, of course, been placed for much larger amounts. During the first ten months of the current fiscal year, we placed orders valued at about $1-6 billion. For the whole twelve-month period I would estimate the figure at close to $2 billion which is about three-fifths of the whole amount we expect will be spent within the three-year period by the Department of Defence Production. Some of these orders have been placed outside of Canada. As far as Canadian industry is concerned, the change from a year ago may be put in this way. On April 1, 1951, Canadian industry was working on defence orders from the Canadian government valued at $500 million; today it is working on orders valued at $1-5 billion.
As I have already said, this past year has been devoted, in large part, to getting ready to fill these orders and others that will be placed in due course. In some instances, particularly where the items are similar to civilian goods, the change-over to defence production is comparatively simple and deliveries do not lag far behind orders. For example, textile procurement is well advanced. Because of the specialized nature of such a large part of the Canadian program, however, new facilities must be created on a large scale.
We have encouraged industry to use existing facilities where possible rather than to build new plants, but some additions have been necessary.
One method by which the necessary additions have been made is through our program of capital assistance. During the first ten months of the current fiscal year-that is from April 1, 1951, to January 31, 1952-we


have made commitments for capital assistance for some 65 projects involving $120 million. Most of the assistance was given to the aircraft industry, which accounts for 27 out of the 65 projects. The remainder is distributed largely among the ammunition industry, electronics and shipbuilding.
By far the largest portion of the $120 million of capital assistance is for the purchase of new machine tools and specialized types of equipment. A considerably smaller amount is designated for plant construction, extension and conversion which, as a matter of policy, we are trying to keep to a minimum. So that there is no misunderstanding, I would remind the house that facilities established through capital assistance are owned by the crown.
The other form of assistance to expansion is accelerated depreciation. This is a very much misunderstood matter. I have heard it suggested that by granting accelerated depreciation the government is making an unwarranted gift of some kind to industry. Anyone familiar with the matter knows that this is not so. All that accelerated depreciation does is to enable companies to write down for tax purposes the value of the particular assets affected somewhat more rapidly than under the ordinary rules.
In the long run, accelerated depreciation does not necessarily involve real loss of tax revenue. It does, however, encourage the industry to go ahead in the knowledge that if the earning power of the asset is likely to drop sharply at the end of the rearmament period the depreciated value of the asset can be brought down to correspond.
We have used the device of accelerated depreciation sparingly and with discretion, and primarily to encourage the expansion of raw material production. The most common case is one where industry believes that, in the absence of this type of assistance, the commercial prospects of the expanded production do not merit the investment.
In the first ten months of the current fiscal year, certificates for accelerated depreciation have been issued for 57 projects involving $173 million.
In many instances, both capital assistance and accelerated depreciation have contributed to a rounding out of our defence industry and to the creation of productive capacity turning out many new items never before produced in Canada. Important as these two measures were for the creation of specific industrial facilities, their scope has been quite small in relation to the very substantial industrial expansion that is currently under way. Capital expenditures covered by these

two measures during the first ten months of the current fiscal year are less than 10 per cent of the investment outlay which Canadian business is expected to make during the current year.
As I said at the beginning of these remarks, the basic decision was taken to keep government controls to a minimum and as flexible as possible. Our objectives were simple. First it was necessary to assure that defence got the necessary priority over civilian needs. At the same time, since the defence program would be a protracted one, we had to do what we could to avoid damage to the civilian economy and to promote its normal growth to an extent consistent with the achievement of the defence goals.
We had had a wealth of experience during the last war with controls and we knew how to carry on a system of detailed allocation of our resources. We recognized we might have to take full advantage of this experience. It was prudent, therefore, to provide the legal basis for full government control over production and distribution and to assemble the nucleus of an administrative staff. This we did under the Essential Materials (Defence) Act late in 1950 and under its successor, the Defence Production Act.
The mere existence of these powers has helped by assuring that defence and defencesupporting industries receive what they need without delay. It has done so, moreover, with economy in terms of men and money, and with little burdensome regulation which businessmen find so frustrating. Should the international situation require it, our existing machinery could be adapted almost overnight to full-scale control and allocation. Conversely, it could be abandoned just as quickly and without most of the difficulties with which we had to contend in the post-war decontrol program. In short, our approach has been flexible and it has worked. That it has worked is due in no small measure to the cooperation of Canadian industry, which has not only supplied us with able administrators, but has conducted its operations in broad conformity with the aims of our policy.
Throughout the past year, government control over domestic steel supplies has been exercised by so directing the production and shipments of domestic steel producers as to ensure that the requirements essential to our defence program were fully met. The remaining supply of steel continued to be distributed by the steel mills and warehouses in a free market to their usual customers. The only exceptions are that we continued in effect an order which virtually bans the use of steel in construction of entertainment,
14, 1952	439
The Address-Mr. Howe commercial, service and like facilities, and we have adopted an inventory control designed to prevent accumulation of unduly large stocks which might be lost to current production or employed in speculative transactions. Supplies received by Canada from the United States under the controlled materials plan must be fully allocated by our own steel division in order to meet our obligations under the plan, and this we have done. The total supply of steel rolling mill products available to ' Canadian industry during 1951 was about 4 million net tons, compared with approximately 3-2 million tons in 1950. This increase resulted from somewhat higher domestic production and from increased imports. At times during the year, acute shortages were experienced in some types of steel and by some industries, so that the larger imports were an important factor in maintaining the output of Canadian manufacturers. While our domestic production this year should be at least as much as in 1951, continued efforts must be made to maintain imports at the level of last year if our minimum steel requirements are to be met. If this is accomplished, we will be able to get through 1952 with no greater difficulties in respect of steel supply than were experienced last year and without any more stringent government control.
Our position in non-ferrous metals differs markedly from that in steel since we are among the world's leading suppliers of most of those metals which are consumed in large volume. As a producer we rank first in nickel, second in aluminum and zinc, and fourth in copper and lead. Our responsibility here, therefore, is not only to see that our own relatively small priority needs are met, but also to do all we can to maximize supplies available for export to the free world. We have discharged our responsibility at home by operating a .purchase approval system under which all domestic purchases are scrutinized and approved or rejected in accordance with the priority of the need and the availability of supplies. This has proved to be a highly flexible system permitting rapid readjustment of civilian domestic supplies to the fluctuating requirements of defence and defence-supporting industries. It has also been most economical. Our international obligations have been met by directing supplies to appropriate destinations through an export permit system and by participation in the international materials conference. Under the aegis of this body, the principal countries of the free world, both producers and consumers, have agreed, in respect of the leading metals, upon quarterly distribution quotas based upon need. By and large the requirements

The Address-Mr. Howe of Canadian industry have been recognized and we have been able to operate within our quotas. The same is true with respect to our quotas of mill forms and other secondary products allocated to us by the United States under the controlled materials plan.
Very recently there has been a noticeable reduction in the pressure of world demand upon available supplies of the leading metals and, unless unpredictable stockpiling operations are undertaken abroad, or unless there is a marked worsening in the world situation, supplies in 1952 should not be as tight as they were last year. I feel confident in saying that our control over supply of these metals in 1951 caused a minimum of dislocation to Canadian producers and consumers and that we may look forward to at least as favourable a result in 1952.
The great developments which have been announced by private enterprise from time to time in the field of mining and metals manufacturing are being pressed forward along a broad front. An increase of 1,150,000 ingot tons to our steel capacity, equivalent to one-third of the actual ingot and casting production in 1951, will progressively be added until all the new facilities are completed early in 1953. This tremendous expansion will result in increased domestic supply of 800,000 net tons of steel rolling mill products for Canadian industry. Canadian production of iron ore will have expanded fourfold between 1951 and 1955, and will be a leading factor in the immense steel expansions now being made in Canada and in the United States. Important expansions are under way in non-ferrous metals, of which the Kitimat venture is by far the largest. The aluminum expansion may be as important, in terms of value of production and exports, as all other non-ferrous developments combined. By 1953, our aluminum capacity will have risen by 35 per cent and if the decision is taken to proceed with the second phase of the Kitimat expansion, capacity may well become two and one-half times as great as in 1951. If present plant materializes, copper production will have increased by 10 per cent in 1955 compared with 1951, nickel will be 15 per cent ahead, lead about 10 per cent, and zinc about 35 per cent. What this means in terms of investment in one year alone is illustrated by the fact that investment intentions in 1953 for mining and related ventures approach $500 million out of a total investment in new capital assets of about $5 billion. We have every reason to take pride in the contribution that these activities will make to the


defence preparations and the maintenance of high level employment both at home and throughout the free world.
This is a convenient point at which to mention that the Department of Trade and Commerce has just completed its annual survey of investment intentions for the year 1952. Total private and public investment is likely to be of the order of $5 billion, involving an increase of just under 10 per cent over the total for $4-6 billion for 1951, which was itself a record year. Perhaps half of the increase over 1951 will represent physical volume and half higher prices.
This is a remarkable indication of the confidence which is being placed in* the future of Canada. When the figures are analysed they also reveal a continued shift towards defence and defence-supporting projects, resources development and utilities, which the government by various means is trying to encourage. For example, I asked that the forecast of capital expenditures be analysed in terms of the deferred depreciation regulations which came into effect at the time of the last budget.
While the trends revealed cannot, of course, be attributed entirely to the effect of the regulations, it is interesting to observe that investment in categories where depreciation is deferred is down about 17 per cent in value and about 22 per cent in volume, whereas investment eligible for the issuance of a certificate of eligibility for current depreciation is up about 34 per cent in value and about 27 per cent in volume.
With the permission of the house, I should like to place on Hansard three tables which summarize the results of several surveys. The first covers production of building materials, past and anticipated. Further expansion in the output of many building materials is planned for 1952. The second table summarizes the results of the survey of private and public investment to which I have already referred, and the third analyses investment intentions for 1952 as they are or are not affected by the deferred depreciation regulations. The first two tables are advance statements of two papers on the building material and investment outlook for 1952 which will be tabled as soon as they become available in printed form.
With the permission of the house, I should like to place these tables on Hansard.

I shall complete these remarks by a few general observations about the Canadian economy as a whole. The past year has been a remarkable one. Twelve months ago the world was in the midst of an inflationary upsurge of prices, from which Canada could not and did not escape. To a large extent that upsurge of prices was based upon fears of imminent all-out war and of the effects of world rearmament. Then came the reaction. Many of the shortages that had been anticipated did not materialize and where shortages did appear they were a good deal less serious than had been feared.
This is the background against which developments in Canada should be viewed. It helps to explain why it is that now, when the defence program is getting into stride and placing real demands upon materials and labour, there should be less pressure on prices and supplies than there was when the defence program was largely on paper and just beginning.
From the outset it was the government's view that defence preparations could be fitted into the economy without an elaborate structure of controls over prices, wages and supplies. I believe the events of the past year support that view. By fiscal, monetary and credit policies, supported by a few controls over essential materials, the government helped to take the steam out of the internal inflationary demands and to restore balance. If, instead of doing this, we had depended mainly upon direct controls we would, I suggest, be worse off now and, in addition, the country would be saddled with a vast bureaucracy of controllers.
Our task now is to maintain a reasonable degree of stability while forging ahead with defence preparations and with the economic development of the country. In many respects the problem is easier than it was a year ago because of the absence of panicky buying. Everyone is a good deal more cautious about the outlook, which is a healthy condition in a free society. Such a condition makes for active competition and a sound price structure. Real trouble is brewing when too many people are convinced either that there is going to be inflation or that there is going to be a depression.
I see no reason to anticipate either inflation or depression. The demand for Canadian output should, in general, be well sustained by the continuing high level of capital investment, by export demand for most of our staple products and by defence preparations. Recent experience, on the other hand, has shown that these demands can be met without undue strain, provided that sensible policies are followed and provided the public does not go in
The Address-Mr. Howe for another buying spree. The recent high level of consumer saving has undoubtedly contributed greatly to the relief of inflationary pressures.
Although we have been passing through a period of what can only be described as very great prosperity, a number of so-called "soft spots" have developed in the economy. As hon. members are aware, there has been a sharp drop in the demand for consumer durables, some textiles and a few other items, and as a result we are contending with some local unemployment and some short time employment. Many reasons are given for these "soft spots" and I am not going to attempt a thorough analysis at this time. It does seem to me, however, that since similar troubles have developed in other countries, particularly in the United States, they cannot be attributed wholly to Canadian conditions or policies, as is sometimes suggested, but must be due in large part to something more fundamental. As long as over-all conditions remain favourable these industries should be able to work out of their difficulties with a minimum of loss.
There is more reason to be concerned about two developments affecting our export trade-the embargo on imports of livestock and meat into the United States resulting from the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, *and the further closing down of markets for Canadian goods in the sterling area. The tightening of trade restrictions around the sterling areas is unfortunate and all of us had hoped that by this time the trend would be in the other direction. However, these latest restrictions are only worse in degree than what we had become used to during the past few years. They are not likely to reduce total trade with the sterling area by very much below what it would have been without the new restrictions, because most relatively unessential items have already been eliminated from our trade with sterling countries. Some producers and manufacturers will, however, feel the pinch.
I have heard the suggestion made in this house that Canada is losing the British market. Of course, that is not true. The fact is that Canadian exports to the United Kingdom increased from $470 million in 1950 to $631 million in 1951 and I would not be surprised if, in spite of the British financial crisis, our exports to that market were to rise by another $75 to $100 million during 1952. Although the British may have to forgo certain marginal items from Canada they are very much interested in items such as our wheat, our flour, our lumber and our metals.
444	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Knight
I shall say little about the embargo on imports of livestock and meat into the United States. This could be a matter of the most serious consequence, but all of us, I am sure, are hopeful that the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease will be brought under control quickly and the embargo removed with the least possible delay.
To conclude, a few words of summary: During the year just passed we have substantially expanded the productive capacity of the country, thus laying a firm basis for rising output of armaments and strategic materials. Deliveries of defence equipment are increasing steadily. The inflationary pressure that was particularly strong in the earlier part of 1951 has eased greatly. National income and employment are at record levels. The Canadian dollar, without official support, has attained parity with the leading world currency. Canadians are prosperous and national savings are very high, in fact almost as high as in the peak years of world war II. There are some clouds on the horizon and I have no doubt that many difficulties will be encountered before the year is out. But, on the whole, the economic outlook for Canada in 1952 is favourable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened to many fine speeches during this debate, among which I would include those of the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply. I should like to congratulate them individually on their respective efforts.
There was another speech delivered last night to which I listened with admiration and envy. I refer to that of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), in which he referred to the need for a different method of redistribution of electoral seats in the House of Commons. Not only did I like the speech for its oratorical quality; I liked it for its subject matter. If I may say so respectfully, I agree with what the hon. member said. I have always felt that our system of redistribution was wrong, that it was a matter for statisticians and technicians rather than politicians. Human nature being as it is I do not see how any man, no matter how honest he may be, can help but be prejudiced in the decision he would make or help to make in the committee when he himself was to gain political or personal advantage, or suffer disadvantage from the decision of that committee. If I were sitting on the other side I think I would say that as readily as I say it from my place at the moment in a section of the opposition.


I feel that this committee should be completely and totally removed from political influence. When I say that, I am not suggesting that the present government has used or is apt to use any more political influence than any other party if it found itself in the government's position. My idea of a committee on electoral distribution would be one headed perhaps by the chief electoral officer, a man who I might almost say is qualified by heredity, and indeed by his own performance up to the present time. Then it should include political scientists, a geographer, an economist, a political historian and statisticians. Such a committee should be handed a map, the latest population statistics and told to sit down to do this work. I was glad that the hon. member for Quebec South made favourable mention of a good friend of mine, a political scientist for whom I have the greatest respect, Dr. Norman Ward, a professor of political science in our own university of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon. I know he has devoted a great deal of study to this matter and has written many articles upon the subject. With the knowledge of this subject which he has he would be an ideal member of a committee such as I have suggested.
Generally speaking, I do not like omnibus speeches. I believe that if a man is speaking and wants to make a good speech he should be imbued with one single idea in which he is particularly and vitally interested. The speech which he delivers should convey to his audience a definite impact of that one single idea. However, the debate in which we are presently engaged is characterized by omnibus speeches, and perhaps I may be pardoned if I make one myself. It is fitting perhaps that there should be provided at least once a session an opportunity when a member of parliament, representing as he does so many people and so many different interests, can present to the country through this house some of the ideas which he picks up during his ever-decreasing sojourns at home. So I do not want to say much about anything, but a little about a lot of things with which the people of my constituency are concerned.
The first thing I want to mention is the disappointment which the people, not only of my own city but of our province, feel at the delay in the construction of the Saskatchewan river project. I know that many reasons can be advanced for this delay. It is most unfortunate that two of the three wise men who we were told were to finally look into this matter are unfortunately ill, and to them I extend my sympathies. Whether or not their illness has anything to do

with the delay in the construction of this project, I am not prepared to say because I do not know.
I read the letter which was sent by the chairman of that three-man commission to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) explaining to him, and presumably to the house through him, why it would not be likely that any positive action in the matter could be taken before another year or so. I interpreted the letter to mean that. It is true that hon. members in the opposition and on the government side want to be sure that what we are doing is feasible and practical and good. Personally I thought that that decision had been made some time ago.
I have no objection to a thorough investigation being made to make quite sure that the project is practical, but what I do object to is the persistence with which this government uses this particular thing as an election project. It has been the members on the government side, particularly the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who more than anyone else have raised hopes in Saskatchewan which were later dashed to the ground. I have had considerable experience in listening to this sort of thing, and I have no doubt that if and when the government does decide that this project is feasible we shall be hearing a good deal about it before the next general election, whenever that takes place.
With all this I am not prepared to withhold from the Minister of Agriculture any credit which is due to him in persuading the other members of the government to get on with this particular project. I have no doubt that it would be to his political interest if he could get the project started. But I do object most strenuously to this thing being dragged out at every election, to promises being made which the promisers must know, because they have inside knowledge, cannot be fulfilled. I urge the government to give every consideration to this particular project so that it may be completed at once if it is proved to be feasible.
The next subject I should like to deal with is the development of the Hudson bay route. Ever since I was first elected in 1945 I have given more time to this matter, both in the house and outside, than to any other thing in which I have been interested. Progress has been made, and I commend the government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) for whatever assistance they have given to help the project along.
I think there are still some things the government might do to further encourage the
The Address-Mr. Knight use of that route. We in Saskatchewan are beginning to feel, if indeed we have not felt it for a long time, that with all the uranium discoveries and the like our future lies in the north. Looking to the future, we feel that we want to have an open seaway to connect us with the old country and Europe; and we want a number of branch lines-I cannot go into particulars today-which will link the country both east and west with that Hudson bay route. I was pleased to learn that last year a record number of bushels were shipped from that port. I have not looked up the figure; but I think it was some seven or eight million bushels, but even that is insufficient to enable this route to stand upon its own feet. We have often heard it said, and we believe with truth, that there is no physical reason why 15 million bushels of grain could not be shipped through that port in a year. I am informed-and I do not stand by these figures because I am speaking from memory-that only some fifty-eight days out of seventy-six were employed during the open season last year. We do know that if we *could put 15 million bushels a year through that port, that route would cease to cost the taxpayers of this country a single cent, and we would accomplish our objective of putting it on its feet.
I was interested to learn that the drying facilities of the Churchill elevator were used to capacity this year, I think for the first time. I do not know enough about the matter to recommend that damp wheat from other parts of the country should be shipped up there to be dried and then shipped back again, because shipped back it would have to be since at the moment there is no outlet for it there. I cannot argue that proposition, but it has been argued1 and once more I draw it to the attention of the government. It is true that some of the finest elevator equipment in the world is to be found at that port. It is true that it has a drying capacity which astonished me when I heard: the figures. It is too bad it is not being used more fully. I presume the elevator is already full of grain, and I presume, or at least I hope, most of that grain was damp wheat collected from the prairies being stored there ready for shipment next season.
I would like to say one thing to those outside this house who may read what I am saying. I am thinking now particularly of our merchants, our wholesalers and distributors of goods in Saskatoon and the district it serves. We can never make a success of that port until we have both an import and an export trade. I think perhaps some of the facilities for import could1 be improved1, to permit incoming boats to be unloaded at the

The Address-Mr. Knight same time outgoing boats are being loaded. There is also a demand that the loading platform have a greater capacity. They can load three ships at once now, and it is felt that these facilities should be extended so it would be possible to load five ships. The same thing goes for storage capacity. I think this year it has been shown that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was quite correct when he once said; speaking of the government elevator at Saskatoon, that even if an elevator of that type were empty at least it provided insurance for a contingency. Well, the contingency is here, and as far as I know both these elevators are full.
Speaking of the government elevator at Saskatoon, I am glad to say the drying plant there is working day and night, seven days a week, and working efficiently. The manager, Mr. Halliwell, very courteously showed me through that plant, where I saw the drying process. With all the controversy we have heard about this wheat, needless to say that was a very interesting visit; and I pay this tribute to the courtesy of those officials.
Unfortunately the situation is not equally good all over the country. I believe those who criticized had some justification for saying the government did not get into action about this thing in time. Even today up in the northern part of the province there is what the Star-Phoenix calls a grim situation. It says that the elevators at White Fox are still plugged1, and that many farmers along that Nipawin-Prince Albert line have not yet been able to sell one solitary bushel of wheat, owing to the fact that the box car situation is just impossible. However, that is outside of my own sphere, outside my own constituency, and I Shall let it go at that.
I should say a word on one or two other matters, and one is the housing situation in Saskatoon. Last year Saskatoon built a good many houses, perhaps more than the average city of its size; but the point in which I think the government should be particularly interested, the situation for which to some extent it is responsible, is that we are at our wits' end to know how to handle the influx of defence personnel coming to our city. We have an advanced air training school there at which, when the project is completed, there will be 800 additional air force personnel. This is just at the edge of our city, at the airport buildings. Strange to say even I have been pestered with letters from many of these men, who I suppose have written to me as a final resort, asking where in the world they might be able to get houses. I went up and looked over that situation and saw the progress that has been made on those buildings. At the present 
time the government has a plan under which it is building large blocks of apartments for single men, and they have potential accommodation-and believe me it is just potential at the moment-for 150 married personnel. The trouble, of course, is that these buildings are only being started, and the officer who showed me around said he thought they would all be ready at the same time but there was very little chance any would be completed before next fall. That is a long time to wait. The city council, having taken, some note of this matter, passed a resolution some time ago, which I imagine has been forwarded to the government. I shall not read the resolution in full, but these are the important parts:
Whereas the city council of Saskatoon always has understood that the provision of housing for the married personnel of the armed services is a federal responsibility, and
Whereas it is understood that some 400 families of personnel coming to the Saskatoon air training school are expected to arrive in Saskatoon during the next few months, and
Whereas only 150 housing units for such families are being provided at the airport, and Whereas there is a housing shortage in Saskatoon which will make it almost impossible for these incoming families to obtain adequate accommodation . . .
Whereas this council on May 28, 1951, passed the following resolution which was forwarded to the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence, and the Minister of Resources and Development: "That the federal government be requested to provide adequate housing accommodation for married service personnel to be completed for occupation as soon as required, the cost to be borne solely by the federal government."
Now, therefore, be it resolved:
"That this council again strongly urges upon the federal authorities the immediate necessity of providing adequate housing accommodation for all families of members of the armed services who may be sent to this city."
I would urge upon the government some serious and practical consideration of the terms of that resolution.
While I am talking about the airport, there is one other matter I would draw to-the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). We have a fine field and very good air service, but there is a lack of catering service. There is talk, and at the moment it is only talk, that the Department of Transport proposes to erect an administration building in connection with that airport. If that is done, no doubt there will be some provision for catering, but at the moment there is none. The board of trade, which is: naturally interested in that sort of thing, has; drawn it to my attention and I think the attention of the Minister of Transport, that such accommodation is necessary for the convenience of passengers originating there and those passing through that city.

In our city we have some packing houses and, naturally, packing house workers. While I am glad to be able to report that there has been no outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in our immediate vicinity-I need not have said "immediate" because the quarantined area is some distance away-there has nevertheless been an adverse effect upon the industry and the people who work in it. First of all, there have been decreases in the prices of cattle. I shall not go into the figures because the decrease has been about the same as took place in Calgary and other western markets. There has been a slackening, only temporary I hope, in the use of packing house facilities. While the plants have not been shut down, this has resulted in some workers being laid off, but not to the extent that has occurred in other places. I believe I have the figures here.
I am quoting from a dispatch of March 6 which says:
Lack of cattle coming to market as a result of the foot-and-mouth disease in southern Saskatchewan has caused Intercontinental Packers (Saskatoon) to temporarily lay off more than twenty employees already and others may be out of work in a few days, G. Willows, manager, said Wednesday.
Unless the situation changed Mr. Willows expected that twenty more employees would be laid off next weekend and an additional twenty the following weekend. About 200 are employed now at the plant.
I can only express the hope that it will not be necessary to render assistance to many of these packing house workers, that is the assistance so eloquently pleaded for by the member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), but the hope too that such assistance will be proffered to those affected.
I have received letters about a matter, and frankly I have no solution for it nor can I suggest a solution. I believe that, in all justice, the situation should be brought to the notice of the government. It concerns certain small truckers-I use the term "small" in the sense that they are not trucking companies but individuals. News of the arrangements between the oil companies and the railroads has caused consternation among these people. While I have no immediate solution to offer, I believe the problem points up the argument that we need some sort of over-all transportation plan in this country. Britain was faced with this problem, but in reverse. It was not the railroads that were putting the truckers out of business, but the truckers that were putting the railroads out of business. The only way that both of them were saved was through an over-all transportation system.
I am thinking of a country district in Great Britain from which you can go by bus
The Address-Mr. Knight to your destination and use your return ticket to come back by rail. The same situation applies, to a large extent, to the shipment of goods. I do not know how successful the system has been, but it would appear that the men who were driving the trucks are still employed. Unfortunately, as I said, this problem concerns individuals as well as companies, and it has made it difficult for the man who is trying to start up in business. One man writes to me, and his letter is dated March 6, in the following terms:
Since returning to Canada from overseas in 1946, I have put in a lot of long hard hours attempting to build a dream into a business. I now own two units, partly financed, and should this "price slashing" agreement be allowed to take effect, there will be only one result. Myself as well as many others in the same boat will be back where we started from, if not worse.
I am not advocating any line of policy in that regard, I am simply bringing the matter to the attention of the government.
There are two other subjects upon which I intended to speak, but perhaps I should change the order of my presentation. There is a rather serious indictment I intended to bring against the Department of National Defence concerning their handling of a certain matter, but I expect my time will have run out before I come to that so I had better leave it until the defence estimates are before us. There are two of these smaller things, which perhaps look small to us but are very important to the people concerned, about which I wanted to say something. The first concerns pensions for the blind. I was favoured by being asked to interview some of the aged blind people who are now in a home for the blind. They drew this to my attention, and I think I should draw it to yours. Blind people are not in as good a position as many other pensioners. I believe that blindness is a disability which should be considered quite apart from the old age pension, just as I believe the disabilities of our burnt-out veterans should be considered quite apart from the old age pension.
As the matter stands now even the burnt-out. veterans, bad as their situation may be, have an advantage over the blind in that the means test does leave them at least a fraction of their military pension to be added to the old age pension. The blind have a pension which is the same as the old age pension, and up to the age of seventy that is subject to the means test. I am going to suggest that, the blind person who reaches that age is more helpless than the ordinary old age pensioner. I believe the solution is the-removal of the means test for blind pensioners. I would go that far. Of course, I do not believe the ordinary old age pensioner should

The Address-Mr. Knight have to live on $40 a month, and I have the more reason not to believe the blind old age pensioner ought to have to live on $40 a month. He has more expenses. He has to have someone to take care of him, and he probably has to live in an institution.
He is precluded from being able to earn a little extra money. I would therefore put that appeal before the house.
There is one other subject that I wish to mention. This time it is one which was drawn to my attention by a lady who is afflicted with deafness, and the matter in question has to do with hearing aids. I wrote to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) with regard to the general idea, advancing to him the proposition that I did not think that hearing aids should be subject to the sales tax. Whatever little money the sales tax upon hearing aids brings into the treasury could very well be done without, I think. In these days of tremendous expansion-the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has been just now painting a hopeful picture-and tremendous investment, and there is a tremendous government surplus this year, can we not do without this little pittance which comes in from the imposition of the sales tax upon these things which, as this lady said, make the difference, practically, between existence and non-existence to the deaf. These people who have to depend upon the hearing aids certainly have no joy in life when they are without them.
I have here in my hand a bill. I may say it is a copy of something issued by the Canadian customs department. It is an invoice for goods. May I point out, first of all, that these hearing devices cost far too much. Some of these little hearing aids that you see-or that you are not supposed to see-in a person's ear cost as much as $200. For some reason or another a great many of them are imported from the United States. Just imagine the predicament of this particular lady or that of any other lady-or of anyone, for that matter-who has to send this thing off to the United States for repairs. These people cannot afford to have two of them. You can imagine the delay involved-delay at the factory, the delay in bond, the notification that the thing is there, the delay in picking it up-the charges collect and all the rest of it. This lady told me that she had to do without this particular hearing aid for three weeks. Can you imagine the result? Can we put ourselves in a situation where you and I could not hear a word for three weeks? What would life be to us under those circumstances?
This lady suggested that she thought this matter was the responsibility of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin).


She did not see why, when we had a department of health in this country, they could not bestir themselves in this matter. If none of these things are now available in Canada, let us make them available here in Canada, and let the department of health have them here in Canada where they would be easily and readily available for the people who need them, in the places where they are needed.
I want to say a word about the imposition of this particular sales tax. I was astonished to find that sales tax had been charged not only upon the new parts which had been charged for by whoever had done the repairing but also on the total repair bill itself; and the total repair bill is marked "repairs only". To substantiate that statement I am going to read some of these charges, Mr. Speaker, and let you see what it costs these people. It must be remembered that these batteries must be renewed from time to time, and you have to send off to the United States for those, and there is another fuss about those before you can get them from the customs and you finally get them back into the machine so that you can hear.
This is a "Canadian customs invoice for goods", et cetera, et cetera. I will not worry you with more of that. It is the invoice for a hearing aid purchased by Mrs. So-and-So, shipped from a point in the United States. I see that St. Paul, Minnesota, is mentioned, and the invoice is marked "express charges collect". In the column headed "marks and numbers on packages" we find "1 carton". Under the headings of "quantities and description of goods" and "selling price to purchaser in Canada" we find the following:
Model 1550, No. 6718S	Service
Replaced microphone	 $5.50
Repair switch	 1.55
Replace condensers	80
Replace resistors	80
Repair receiver	 7.00
Labour on transmitter	 3.50
Then we find in big writing down below: Above instrument being returned alter repair only.
I think maybe that was a slight prevarication but I find the word "only" is underlined. Then we find the words: "C.O.D.; express charges collect". It has been through the customs, lying there for a while, and it is stamped at a later date by the Department of National Revenue of Canada: "Duty paid, February 19, 1952." Then the name of the officer is given, and so on.
This is a copy of the original. The total bill that this lady had to pay for the repair of the hearing aid was $19.15. Then it says here: "10 per cent-$1.92", which is what she had to pay before she got the thing.

I do not know, but I am just putting it up to the minister, or to whoever is concerned, whether that is the sort of treatment that should be accorded to people who are suffering from their particular disability, namely deafness. What have we a Department of National Health and Welfare for anyway?
I think that covers most of these things which I shall not describe as minor because they are major items to the people concerned.
My hon. friend tells me that I have only two minutes left. I shall therefore reserve for a later date my little quarrel with the Department of National Defence.
