speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, may I say that I have certain views that I have been wanting to put before this house for a considerable length of time. Before I start, I should also like to congratulate the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I think they did an excellent job.
In going around my constituency I meet a great number of people; and of course they give me their different views. Those views always have a bearing on my thinking. I do not always agree with them, but quite a number of the ideas are quite sound. This thinking, if it is directed in the right channels, does no harm. Inasmuch as farmers are hard workers, if they think that those in any other group are getting more than their fair share, their state of mind is not a satisfied one. I want to say this. Because our young folks sometimes think there are other pastures that are greener, and are leaving the farms in great numbers, the parents are having quite a hard time to hold their sons and daughters on the farm. The farmers, being hard workers, do not necessarily envy any other group. We are therefore not going to look at the situation in that light. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the west has many disadvantages because we are far from the best markets of the world or from the east; and anything that causes disturbance to or disrupts our way of life, we take seriously. We have a transportation problem, a grain problem and now, of course, we have the problem of the hoof-and-mouth disease which is going to cause hardship not only to the people in the areas concerned but to all farmers in our country. These problems are not always easy to solve. We cannot necessarily blame the weather on any particular person, but certain things are going on in Canada today that are apt to cause more or less trouble, and I shall be coming to them shortly.
The Address-Mr. Hetland
I know our cost of living is high. Our dollar also is not worth as much as it was years ago. The C.C.F. party say that profits are too high. I remember a year ago, when this government was putting the corporation tax up to 49 per cent, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) said that he was very much opposed to it. I do not believe that profits are the cause of our high cost of living. When Sir Stafford Cripps was chancellor of the exchequer in England during the Labour party's time in office he said in Maclean's magazine on November 1, 1949, that if he took all the profits from the corporations it would amount to only 4 pence in the pound, and he did not think it was worthwhile; it would do more harm than good.
Because the cost of living is high, the unions are always asking for more wages. They say they must have more wages in order to live. If they want an increase of 15 cents an hour they ask for 30 cents and they usually get it. When the 48-hour week was cut down to 40 it had a bearing on the cost of living. Before I go any further I want to say I am not against the union man. Strikes are not between the employer and the employee any more. Possibly they were years ago. They are now between the citizens of this country and the group that is striking.
I remember that when the railroad strike was over Mr. Hall was reported in the press as having said that the railroads got the worst of the deal. It was not the railroads that got the worst of the deal, Mr. Speaker, it was every man, woman and child in this country.
Some hon. members may say to me that I voted to settle the strike. I did because we in the west had our crops ready to harvest, and if the strike had gone on very much longer we would have been out of fuel, repairs and everything. It would certainly have caused a tremendous loss. I consider that the farmers had more or less a loaded weapon pointed in their direction while that strike was on. Where is all this going to end? That is the reason I am speaking today. The men are now asking for another 36 cents an hour increase, according to the press. If this thing keeps going on, a wage of $50 to $60 a day will be quite common and we shall also have to pay $50 to $60 for a pair of shoes, and I do not see where we shall be any better off.
I know that many union leaders are good men, but quite a few of them have not yet grown up. When a strike is on there does not seem to be any sympathy for the average citizen of this country. Let me tell you about a certain incident that happened to one of my constituents. He had sold his old combine

The Address-Mr. Hetland and had ordered a brand new one. The combine came into his town, and before he could get it unloaded the strike was on. This farmer tried every possible means to get the combine unloaded. He was refused. He went to the labour leaders and they said: "No, absolutely not; we are out to cause as much confusion as possible." This farmer went home very indignant, I can tell you. After the strike was settled the combine was unloaded. It took him another two days to get it in order to be put into the field. The farmer worked night and day trying to get his crop in, but before he was half through with his crop the weather broke and half the crop was left in the fields. The next spring, because of the water in the low places and the damage caused by mice and deer, and what-have-you, the crop was not worth cutting. All that the farmer could do was to set a match to his crop. That farmer told me that it would take him years to catch up to what he lost in the fields during this strike. I could go on and tell of many other instances, but I do not think hon. members are very interested in that. This is a glaring example and I wanted to bring it before the house. Again I emphasize that I am not against unions. I want to make that very clear. I think that unions have done a lot of good in this country. I can easily understand the position of a f ather with a family. He wants to be sure of a job and he wants to have a decent wage so that he can feed and clothe his family. We all understand that. It is against human nature for a man to get married and start raising a family and not know whether he can feed them or not. Most union men are reasonable and not in favour of strikes. They know that you cannot get something for nothing.
I have another matter that I should like to bring before the house. I still think that in our unions we have an element that is out to hinder as much as possible our way of life. Before I go any further I should say that the cost of living is to be blamed on wages continually going up. When a man takes an axe on his shoulder and a saw under his arm and goes into the woods and starts cutting down a tree he is in this position. If you double his wages and double the wages of all the men down the line the cost of your house will rise in proportion to the rise in wages.
I should like to say a word on social benefits. You cannot get all these social benefits without raising our taxes. I was very interested in the speech of the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Catherwood). I think he used a lot of common sense. I shall read
(Mr. Hetland.]
from his speech as reported on page 220 of Hansard of March 7. He said:
I do say, however, and I emphasize this very strongly, that there is a limit to the amount of taxation which the people of the country can bear.
I agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he pointed out yesterday that the limit had been reached, but I also say it has been passed. The government must realize more seriously than ever before how dangerously we are riding the crest of an inflationary spiral. The time has come when we in this parliament, and the government particularly, have got to consider retrenchment because the days of buoyant revenue will not be with us to the extent they have been during the past year.
I agree with that, but I am glad that it came from the official opposition. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is not worried about spending. He likes to spend the taxpayers' money. He is always asking for more benefits, but cries to high heaven when the taxes are raised. You cannot have it both ways.
When the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan came to power they thought that, so far as spending money was concerned, the sky was the limit. But after having been in office for some time they now find that they cannot go any farther until they have more revenue and have opened up more sources of revenue. It makes a difference when a party is in power, especially if it has made a few bad deals.
Unemployment insurance is good for the labouring man; I think it is a wonderful thing. But that, too, costs money. I understand that 40 per cent of unemployment insurance is paid by the employee, 40 per cent by the employer and 20 per cent by the government. We see that 60 per cent of that is not paid by the employee; it must come from some other source. The 40 per cent the employer pays must be added to the price of his article, thus bringing up the cost of living. The 20 per cent paid by the government must be raised through taxation, with resulting increased taxes.
I have no quarrel with the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) when he says that these unemployment insurance benefits should be increased. However in that speech he has blamed the government for high taxes, and has described taxation as plundering. At the same time he calls for more benefits. The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Catherwood) and the hon. member for Broadview should get together, so that they may be more consistent.
One finds if he goes to a city that he cannot induce any of these unemployed men to come out on the farm. A friend of mine went to a city in Saskatchewan where there were 400 unemployed men. He wanted a man

to help do the chores during the winter months, so that the employer might take it a little easier. When a request was made, the official in charge just laughed. He said, "We have not a man in this group here who will go out on the farm." I do not blame the unemployed men for not going on the farm, because the farmer cannot afford to pay the benefits the worker can receive in the city. If the farmer did pay those benefits, farm prices would have to be raised considerably. Where would we go from there?
But if I were unemployed and had a family to support I certainly would go on a farm during the winter months, or until I could get something better. I am wondering whether we are spoiling some of our working groups. Some members of the opposition say that all labour should belong to unions. I have no fault to find with that suggestion; I believe it is true. I believe also that if all labour belonged to unions, farmers included-and we have our unions-we would not see strikes, where one class gets more than is coming to it. We know if the spread gets too wide between the higher and lower paid groups, the lower paid groups must take a lower standard of living. It may be that the farmers should belong to one union. But what would happen if the farmers went on strike? If we held up food production and did not permit it to go to the cities, inside of two weeks people by the thousand would be starving. Would that be right?
Labour says that strikes are right and fair; but I say it would be just as fair for the farmer to keep at home the products of his farm. I do not think the government would stand idly by and let that happen, and I would not blame it for taking action, because we know that two wrongs never make a right. We must keep in mind however that the farmers have a weapon; and if they went on strike it would make the weapon of the labour unions appear mighty small.
It may be that I have gone too far in discussing this matter, but I am anxious that there be no misunderstanding. I repeat my belief that labour should receive a fair wage and all the benefits it can get, provided all groups receive the same. On the other hand I do not believe it is fair for some groups to work 40 hours in the week while others work 80.

I am opposed to strikes that cause untold misery and endanger lives. I am against strikes that are caused by irresponsible men who I think are out to cause as much delay as possible in our defence efforts. These men are not Canadians and I believe they should be punished in the same degree as our other sons and daughters who do not belong to unions.

I left in ample time but even the government could not control the weather and we were delayed. I have read both speeches and I find that they equal, if they do not excel, what I expected from both hon. gentlemen.
As the first representative of our province to speak in this debate I should like to say that with the members from other provinces who have spoken, we from Newfoundland are equally sorrowful at the death of our late king. There is one little story which I think is most explanatory. This was set out in a letter which appeared in the press in Newfoundland written by a doctor. He described how he had been called to go to one of the outports outside of St. John's. When he got there he found that the blinds were drawn in all the houses. He asked the first person he met when his patient had died. The reply was, "No one has died, sir; that is for our king." I think that is very descriptive of the feeling in Newfoundland and our connection with the crown.
With other hon. members of this house we are proud of our new sovereign, Queen Elizabeth. We were glad to hear from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) the other evening that there is to be no disturbance of what we in Newfoundland believe is the title of this country-the Dominion of Canada. We are most conservative in Newfoundland, even though so far all of us are not Progressive Conservatives. I repeat that we are most conservative about the old traditions. As the cornerstone of the empire, as the oldest colony of Great Britain, we do hope that these old traditions will be retained.
I do not propose to deal extensively with the speech from the throne but rather with matters chiefly provincial. I trust that for the next couple of years hon. members will understand that, until the newest province is fully integrated into the dominion, much lea-way will be allowed in presenting our problems. Because of the newness of our province it is only by constant repetition that hon.

members will be able to appreciate the difficulties we face which are not common to all of Canada.
As I say, I do not intend to speak extensively about the speech from the throne but I do want to say that I endorse fully the remarks made by my leader during this debate. Despite what has been said in a derogatory way about that speech, and unfortunately I did hear a few smart-Aleck remarks from the opposite side, I consider his to be the finest speech made in this debate.
I agree with my leader's request that the question of the Lisbon conference should be the subject matter of a separate debate. I agree further that defence should be the subject matter of a separate debate. It would be a great pity if by any chance- there have been some suggestions in the last few days that this is to happen-these important subjects became submerged in this debate. As is quite evident from a number of speeches that have been made, and as will be evident from the one I am about to make, the subjects generally dealt with in this debate are referred to as parochial matters. That is all the more reason why we should have two separate debates, one on the Lisbon conference and the other on defence. I do not know whether that has been agreed to, but I think it should be.
I understand also from the speech from the throne that a measure for the redistribution of the representation in this house is to be introduced at this session. After having listened to the very fine speech of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) last evening, I think the government might very well take his advice. I believe the hon. member is the dean of this house in length of service and for that reason, quite apart from his own brilliant self, his remarks should carry great weight. It would be a shame if his arguments against gerrymandering were not heeded by the government, because I believe he showed pretty conclusively that governments which have gerrymandered in the past have not benefited from such tactics.
I also understand, for what it is worth, that the introduction of this measure would indicate that there is to be no election this year. Whether that is so remains to be seen, of course; but that view appears to be buttressed by the fact that the Prime Minister is not going to advocate any of Dr. Abbott's soothing syrup in the way of reduced taxation. If that is so, if we are not to have any reduction in taxation, this government is going to be in an extremely difficult spot not only this year but until they decide the time is right to introduce such a measure. We-and by that
The Address-Mr. Higgins I mean not only members of this house but the people of Canada-have put up with this high taxation because we were told it was necessary because of defence commitments and in order to aid our allies. This afternoon the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) delivered a very lengthy speech. I could not follow him too clearly, but I did take some notes as he went along and I believe he said that in his department alone some $200 million will remain unexpended this fiscal year. If that is the case in one department of government, how much unexpended money may there be in all the other departments taken together? And what is the reason for making these tax collections? Why were these vast sums of money taken from the taxpayers of the country if they are not to be spent? I believe the government has a good deal of explaining to do in this connection, but so far I have not heard an explanation.
This afternoon we heard a most peculiar statement by the Minister of Defence Production, something which frankly I never expected to hear in this house. Before I had the pleasure of coming here as a member the reputation of the minister even in Newfoundland had been that of a man who knew exactly where he was going and what he was doing. Certainly since I have been here he has rather enhanced his reputation along that line. He is a Caesar as to whose actions there can be no question; but what did we find this afternoon? I may not quote his words exactly, but I think I have them pretty well as he said them. His staiement was; "Looking back, we could not have known a year ago what we know now; and we now agree that some things should be done differently." To me at least that was a tremendous confession, the idea of the minister admitting that he could have made a mistake. Something must have gone wrong with the government machine. We can laugh at ministers now and again. We can enjoy remarks they make. We may even enjoy seeing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) make such grave errors as he has made. But when the Minister of Defence Production makes an error we see the whole fabric of government begin to shake. I am sure it must have caused shivers to run down the backs of hon. members opposite. After all, this is the one minister to whom no one dares say anything, yet now he admits this mistake. Why he does it I do not know. Could it be that he is getting more mellow, or what is the reason? I am sorry he is not here to answer. I do not suppose he would reply except to say, as he said the last time I spoke, "Carry on, young fellow. You are doing as well as you can." As a newcomer here, as one who had

The Address-Mr. Higgins such a very high opinion of the minister, and still has in view of all he has done in the past, I found it most peculiar that he should now be making grave errors and, above all, admitting them.

I am talking with the Minister of Public Works again for a moment. From the beginning, at the time when we first came up here in 1949, I made the request to him for a wharf. I hate to mention small matters. This is the biggest wharf in our province, with all due respect to those wharves that have been constructed at Bonavista, Twillingate and even the one in the constituency of my friend, the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick). They have all had grants for wharves and they are well justified, but when I see the condition of that greatest wharf of the whole lot, the pier that is used by all the people of Bell island-last year some 100,000 people used that wharf as well as motorcars; in fact, everything that is transported from the iron isle, which has the biggest iron mine in the British empire, I might say, has to go over that wharf-then I have to come back and ask the minister what goes on. As to the last time anything was done in this connection, I remember we started on it in 1949. He has been making the excuse to me that it is a ferry wharf and he cannot help me. On July 20, 1950, the acting minister at that time was the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) and he wrote to Mr. Curtis, who is our attorney general. In the last paragraph of his letter he says:
In some cases where the maintenance of a wharf has been shown to be in the public interest in addition to its being used for ferry purposes, the federal and provincial governments have combined forces and built a structure common to both. It might be possible for this government and yours to reach some such agreement in the case of Portugal Cove but unless and until some such agreement is reached, the maintenance of this wharf will be considered your responsibility.
I would plead with the minister at this time that he should think it is his responsibility and try to get together with the government of the province. I think he is fairly close to that government in a number of ways. At all events he is closer than I am.


In that way we might get something done. But I impress upon him the fact that one of these days that wharf is going to collapse. It is the only way that a community of 10,000 people who use the wharf daily have of getting all they need to eat and everything else, and it is their only way of getting to the mainland of the province. I would ask the minister to bear it in mind.
While we are passing out compliments, I should like to thank the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) for arranging T.C.A. direct service from Montreal. It is not quite direct, but it is a great improvement over the previous service. It stops only at Moncton and Sydney. The people of the newest province will be exceedingly grateful to him.
The other day I asked the Minister of Labour, who is not quite hearing me yet, a question: Is labour being recruited by the Fraser-Brace Terminal Construction Company at Saint John, New Brunswick, for work in Newfoundland and Labrador? Unfortunately I asked "Is labour being recruited?" and the minister said, "No." The question now is: Have they recruited it? I asked that question because the information that has been given-and there have been some kicks about it-is that considerable labour has been imported or at least recruited and brought down to work in Newfoundland and Labrador on radar stations. There has been some protest in that connection. With all due respect to the speech from the throne, and what it says about employment being high, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we can do with a lot of jobs down in our part of the country yet. I would ask the minister to keep that fact in mind; I would say this: When they get short down there, then send some labour from other provinces; but do not send them down until that time comes. I also wish to make a plea for Saint John, New Brunswick, as well. I do not want Saint John, New Brunswick, to feel that I am not thinking of them, because the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) made a very touching plea the other day. I want to support him in every way I can. I do not know, but even the Saint John harbour salmon must have been touched by the plea of the hon. member. He is not in his place tonight, but I certainly support him, Mr. Speaker.

In conclusion, I might also say that the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) made reference to storm damage, as did the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth (Mr. Kirk). I understand that as a result of very severe damage done to the fishing community in Labrador in December last, and

also at Port au Port, representation has been made to the government. I do want to add my voice to the voices of the other hon. members and also to the voice of the government of Newfoundland in asking that due recognition be given to the people in those areas because the damage was quite severe. I believe that, because the present finances of the province are so grievously impaired by the continuous inroads made on them by the present government of Newfoundland, it is going to be very difficult to meet demands of this kind.
Briefly I should like to bring a matter to the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). A project is to be established, or an attempt is to be made to establish a project in Newfoundland by the name of the Sieg-heim proposition. It is proposed-I do not know whether it is actually going to be done or not but the necessary act was passed last year-to incorporate a company to carry on a woods operation in Labrador. I have an advertisement in my possession, which was circulated through the woods labour offices in Germany, asking for 400 German woodsmen to work in Labrador and to be paid at the rate of $3.50 a cord. They are to be fed a type of food similar to dehydrated German army food, and they are to be housed in canvas camps. The camps are already in storage in St. John's. I would make this protest at this time to the minister. That type of labour should not be permitted to be imported into Canada.
I have three other matters. On a number of occasions we Newfoundland members have asked the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) questions with respect to the depletion of the Grand Banks, and he has assured us on different occasions that there is no evidence of depletion, or at least no evidence to warrant any conservation measures. It is most significant that this year Dr. Templeman of the fisheries research board has made a report on the depletion of the haddock fishery by draggers on the Grand Banks and the figures that he gives are startling, to say the least. He says that the shrinkage in haddock exports from 5,700,000 pounds in the first six months of 1950 to 1,300,000 in the corresponding period in 1951 shows quite clearly what a great danger we are facing in the depletion of these Grand Banks. I see the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Fisheries in his seat. I trust that he will draw this matter to the attention of the minister, who on several occasions has told us that there was no depletion of the Grand Banks. Dr. Templeman's statement is a most serious one. The Grand Banks are the largest reserve that we have 55704-30'
The Address-Mr. Higgins on this side of the water and it is one of the most important assets of the dominion. I trust that he will take the necessary precaution in connection with it.
Another matter has to do with the seal fishery. On December 18 a decision was handed down by the international court of justice at The Hague with respect to the headland rule. By that decision it would appear that the province of Newfoundland is entitled to keep foreign sealers, shall we say, outside its harbours and bays. In other words, the headland to headland should apply. That should apply not only to sealers but to trawlers as well. I hope that the salmon report of Mr. Menzies will be implemented. I cannot refer to it any more than that.
The final matter that I have to bring up has to do with the case of Dr. Sennewald. I am not saying very much on this because it is too long a story, but I received an answer the other day in connection with this matter that to me at least brings the government into it equally with the province of Newfoundland. The Sennewald story is as follows. On November 22 the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), I believe by misinformation from the premier of Newfoundland, authorized a Canso aircraft to be dispatched from St. John's to Gander, carrying a German national of the department of economic development. That aircraft intercepted another German national who was coming out to Newfoundland to explain the whole industrial program of the Smallwood government. From correspondence with him it was quite clear that Dr. Sennewald had very important information to give in connection with these industries. But, if I may use an American expression, the snatch was put on him and he was kidnapped. I could say a lot more about that, but the chief objection I have to make now is that I as a member of the other political party in Newfoundland feel that it was bad enough to have that happen, but when we have a bill for the plane being sent to the province of Newfoundland and I as one of the taxpayers of that province have to pay the bill for the aircraft sent out by the premier of Newfoundland to snatch this German, it is a little bit too thick.
I have exhausted my time. I am very grateful to hon. members for having listened to me as I outlined these many troublesome problems.

I have heard of the damage that has

In connection with that I have since picked up a clipping, to which I now refer. It contains the words of Dr. Anderson, who is chief chemist of the board of grain commissioners in Winnipeg, the man who looks after the actual testing of wheat, after it has been dried. This is what the article in the Western Producer of March 6 has to say under the heading "Farm Driers Do Pretty Good Job":
Fifty-three farm grain driers have been reported operating in the three prairie provinces, Dr. J. A. Anderson, chief of the board of grain commissioners' research laboratory, said last week.
"On the whole they are doing a pretty good job," he said.
It was estimated there were about 30 additional driers on the prairies which haven't been spotted yet.
Samples of dried grain had been received from 31 of the driers, said Dr. Anderson, and in the majority of cases tests showed that operators were successful in avoiding damage to the grain passing through the driers.
Of the 53 driers reported so far, only four are of the type declared unfit for drying milling wheat.
The majority of the farm plants are located in Saskatchewan.
Estimates of the amount of damp grain that can be handled by the average farm drier were placed

at about 1,000 bushels a day. At that rate 50 driers could handle about 5 million bushels in a 100-day period.
Then it goes on to explain:
Elevator agents at country points were selecting one of their number to assume responsibility for gathering and forwarding to the Winnipeg laboratory samples of grain before it goes through the drier, and samples of grain after drying. Results of laboratory tests are wired back to the selected agent. Seventy-two samples were tested by the laboratory in one day last week.
Dr. Anderson said there still were a few "sour spots" but they would be cleared up as they were revealed by laboratory tests.
In my opinion that is quite different from the statement made by the minister. I am sure he has no intention whatsoever of damaging any more the wheat industry of Canada. Apparently however he did not have accurate information.
Another matter with which I wish to deal is one that has been brought up by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth (Mr. Kirk), the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) and the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). These men support the fishing industry and,
I believe, have given an accurate picture of the condition of that industry. Speaking as one who knows nothing whatever about the fishing industry I can still see that they have a just claim for what might be called a national calamity, so far as damage done by the storms last December is concerned. I understand similar storms have wreaked havoc on the equipment of those fishermen in days gone by and, so far as I am concerned and also the other members of this group, I can say that we are wholeheartedly in support of the giving of some help to these fishermen. It does not matter whether they may be on the west coast, the east coast or in central Canada.
I believe the hon. member for Charlotte, however, does not know anything about farming-although he did1 not admit it. During the discussion he had this to say, as reported at page 378 of Hansard-and I am sorry he is not in his seat to hear what I have to say-
Half of these people who go down to the sea in ships produce this food under conditions under which a fanner would turn his back. I am speaking from experience, because I have been on the water both winter and summer. I did not go out on the water for six or eight months, and then take my family south for the winter. I did not go on the water for six or eight months and then sit by the fireside for the remainder of the year. I was on the water twelve months of the year, and I believe I am in a position to understand just what these men have gone through, down through the years.
I would understand from what the hon. member has said, judging by his previous references to agriculture, that he is simply

repeating the old story that has been told in this house for many years, to the effect that the farmers in the prairie provinces work for five or six or eight months in the year and then take their families south. I would tell the hon. member for Charlotte that in his industry the fishermen do not have to feed or milk the fish, but in the cattle industry, in farming, the farmers have to work 365 days in the year, and there is no getting away from it. We do have to feed our cattle, horses, hogs and poultry every day, and the cows have to be milked twice each day, including Sundays. So I am just giving that piece of information to the hon. member, because it would seem that he is somewhat uninformed along these lines.
However I do have a lot of respect for the hon. member for Charlotte. He is the one who has had courage enough to come out here and make a plea on behalf of the industry he represents. He has also had courage enough to tell us about some of the injustices that exist as regards prices in the United States and Canada. He tells us that he lives on the border, and that he crosses over on frequent occasions. Before I leave that subject let me say that this group is in sympathy with the request made by those three members, and they will have our wholehearted support in their demands of the government.
Later in his speech he dealt with a number of subsidies which, he suggested, were enjoyed by farmers. However, anyone who will take the trouble to go through the list will see that many city and town people enjoy benefits from those subsidies, as well. And it might not be out of order or out of place to remind all members that when agriculture is prosperous, all Canada benefits. Organized labour, or unorganized labour, would benefit from profits on the farms. If a farmer has not the money to buy the products of industry then those who are engaged in other lines of industry are soon laid off from their work and find themselves drawing unemployment insurance-and if they are not in that class they must go without.
Then, in his speech he read from a booklet published by the Department of Agriculture, which said this:
New activities in the postwar period include a commitment on the part of the dominion government to support farm prices. The Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944 states:
"In prescribing prices the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations."
The Address-Mr. Fair

It is true that there are supported prices for the packers, and others in that line.

We have been kidded along, deliberately or otherwise, by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and his parliamentary assistant that that price is effective. That is not correct. Only last night the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) made a speech in the French language. This morning I was reading the translation of his speech to be found on page 427 of Hansard for yesterday. These remarks, which I will quote later, completely contradict the statement that has been made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and his parliamentary assistant (Mr. McCubbin). The hon. member for Beauce had this to say:
Last Saturday I was visited in my home by a group of farmers from the parish of St. Honore de Beauce. They had brought me a request which they had circulated in great haste among their friends, the hog producers of the district. In a few hours this request was covered with 165 signatures.
St. Honore is an average agricultural parish in my constituency. The farmers are relatively prosperous because they are hard-working, thrifty, and because they know how to turn to account the small income afforded by their calling. I repeat that in one parish, in the space of a few hours, 165 hog producers asked to have their grievances brought to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) through their representative in Ottawa.
And what do they ask? Briefly this: that in view of the price of mill feed, the floor price of 26 cents a pound for pork is much too low; that, moreover, the floor price is not maintained in the Quebec market.

Some may refer to provincial autonomy but, for my part, I am indifferent to that providing the farmers get a reasonable price for their products. As a matter of fact, X have in my hand forty-one copies of invoices given me by these good farmers, and I see that in the weeks of February 25 last and March 3, those farmers were paid at the Legrade, Inc., packing plant in Quebec city, 20 cents a pound for class A hogs and 19-6 cents for class B-l.

I also received yesterday a letter from another producer in my county, Mr. Gerard Veilleux of Ste. Clothilde de Beauce. If I had the time, I could quote from that letter and I think I could prove, by the figures submitted, that that gentleman lost the sum of $58.61 on the sale of four hogs.
I wonder where the Minister of Agriculture and his parliamentary assistant are with their enforcement of the laws of this country? That is a condition that exists in Quebec, and I know a similar condition exists in Alberta. I do not doubt that similar cases can be cited as having occurred in other provinces. The hon. member continued:
Confronted by those stupendous facts, I went to the extent, yesterday morning, of writing a message to the packing house of the Co-operative Federee, in Quebec, in order to find out what is going on in that establishment. I wrote:
"Could you let me know what price was paid for hogs, grades A and B, which reached packing house, February 23, and March 3,	4 and 5?"
Soon afterwards, I received a most courteous answer, stating:
"Since February 16, we pay grade A hogs support prices Quebec 251, grade B 25.10."
Naturally, I looked around for some sound explanation of the whole business; I contacted an official in the department, right here in Ottawa. To my great surprise, he told me a thing I did not know; it appears that throughout Canada neither the merchants nor the packers have to pay the minimum price of 26 cents set by the agricultural prices support board. I must confess that I have wondered whether I had misunderstood -the matter and a few hours later, I again turned to the same official who gave me the same answer.
I am asking the Right Honourable Minister of Agriculture to enforce, if possible, the payment of that floor price to producers. I also ask him to raise this price at least to 28 cents a pound, for even at that the farmer would produce at a loss.


I received lately a resolution passed by the U.C.C., a southern Quebec federation, which reads as follows:
February 7, 1952
"At a meeting held at St. Joseph de Beauce on February 6, 1952, and which was attended by about 300 farmers representing 35 unions of the U.C.C. of southern Quebec."
Thirty-five unions, that's something for sure.
"Resolved that whereas the price of pork has fallen disastrously the meeting registers a strong protest against this situation.
Claims from the agricultural prices support board a minimum price of 28 cents."
The hog producers of this country feel that 28 cents should be the minimum paid for grade A. hogs. Further on the hon. member had this to say:
The official of whom I was speaking a moment ago went further. He told me: "It is up to the farmers to look after their own business and not to sell to those who do not pay the floor price." That is a fine answer, Mr. Speaker.
I am saying now, as I have said before on many occasions, that the farmers have no guaranteed floor prices for hogs, butter, cheese or eggs at the producer level. It is true that there are prices provided for the packer, but I feel that the experience of the past indicates that they are well able to take care of themselves. Perhaps, as has been suggested here on many occasions, an investigation into the whole packing industry would be a good thing and give to the farmers many millions of dollars to which they are properly entitled. We are told that the budget will be introduced soon and I have some information I should like to pass on to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). No doubt the Minister of Finance has a number of statisticians and mathematicians at his command, but some of the information I am prepared to pass on may give them some other ideas. A number of people seem to have only one-track minds. An advertisement came out this morning put out by the Canadian Home Laundry Manufacturers Association. I do not intend to quote all of it, but there is some interesting information I should like to refer to the attention of the minister. It is headed, "Does the Government Want Less Revenue?" Then it goes on to give the sales of washing machines in certain months in 1951 as follows:
January	 29,528
February	 24,818
March	 27,042
April	 26,754
May	 21,251
June	 14,598
July	  11,539
August	   10,489
It will be noted that April was the month in which the budget was brought down which

increased the sales tax and placed a 15 per cent excise tax on washing machines, stoves, refrigerators and so on. The advertisement goes on:
Note the constant reduction in washing machine purchases after April, 1951, when the 15 per cent excise tax was imposed by the government. Higher taxes are being collected for each machine sold-but with sales down by more than half, does the government really profit by those unreasonable taxes?
They go on to provide the answer, and show that average sales in January and February, 1951, were 27,129 units from which the estimated government revenue from direct taxes, which meant the sales tax only, was $238,735. The average for November and December, 1951, which was long after the excise tax had been applied, was 10,242 units. The sales tax plus the 15 per cent excise tax on those units, amounted to $225,324, or a decrease of a little over 15 per cent after the second tax was applied.
I am not going to quote more from this advertisement; no doubt the minister has had a copy supplied to him. But perhaps we should not blame the excise tax entirely. I believe the prices of many items of electrical equipment are far too high. To support that, all I have to do is quote the recent trade-in prices that have been placed upon old articles from the kitchen, perhaps an old butcher knife or what have you, for which anywhere from $10 to $50 or $60 has been offered as a trade-in. In the case of refrigerators I have seen advertisements in the Edmonton Journal offering as much as $175 for an old butcher knife, an old cup, or something of the kind. That is a definite admission by the manufacturers of electrical appliances that their prices were far too high. Regardless of what anyone may say, this latest development is the result of the resale price maintenance legislation passed last year. I am reminded that the Minister of Finance calls that inflation. Not one of the four or five methods the minister has brought in to deal with that problem has been effective in curing inflation in Canada.
There is another small item that the youngsters of this country are yelling about; that is the 7 cents they have to pay for a bottle of pop. We had that tax on during the war, but after the war it was removed. Kiddies all over the country yelled about that additional tax. They may have a nickel to spend, but they cannot buy their bottle of pop. The excise tax on chocolate bars and gum was reduced to 15 per cent, and there is no direct tax on ice cream, chocolate drinks, popsicles, freshies, and so on. I would ask the Minister of Finance to be good to

Mr. Speaker, I realize that hon. members of this house are anxious to have this debate brought to a conclusion this evening, and for that reason I have agreed with the house leader to make my remarks fairly brief. First may I join with other members in congratulating the mover (Mr. George) and seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. These two hon. gentlemen acquitted themselves in a way that brought honour not only to themselves but to the constituencies they represent.
The speech from the throne has made reference to the loss of our late sovereign King George VI. His late majesty was indeed loved by all Canadians; and although we no longer believe in the divine right of kings I do feel that in so far as our late monarch was concerned there was a certain divinity that surrounded him. The king in many respects was like any one of us. The knife of the surgeon had the same effect upon him that it would have upon us. But to me our monarch represented something more than just the head of the British commonwealth of nations, the greatest organization the world has ever seen. To me our monarch and our present queen represent the long history of the development of British institutions which are the very basis of our way of life in Canada and under which, regardless of what church we may go to, what occupation we may follow or from whence our parents may have come, we find freedom, justice and equal opportunity to all. I do believe that with the coming to the throne of Queen Elizabeth Canada has before it a new era of development and prosperity.
During the course of this debate some controversy has arisen over the statement

The Address

Mr. Decore by the C.C.F. national council on the 5th of this month. For purposes of the record I quote that statement again:
While continuing to support Canada's participation in NATO, the C.C.F. is opposed to certain recent developments in this organization.
Then it went on:

Mr. Speaker, I was amazed at the last speaker's placing such great faith in Tim Buck. Judging by his speech, he appears to be a good student of Tim Buck and communists in general, something which I am not. Possibly he is closer to the communist thought than I am and is therefore better able to speak on that subject. Later on one of my colleagues will answer him and do so satisfactorily. After listening to the last speaker, I feel that the Liberal party are exceedingly fortunate that the C.C.F. published a platform; although they disagree with it, it has been the basis of nearly all their talks up until now. That is natural, in the absence of a program of their own to discuss. I hope they will make the best of it while it is still fresh.
I am not going to waste time by discussing that subject tonight because I have a subject which, to my mind, is a far more important one, as it deals with the fruit and vegetable industry of my constituency. I make no apology for taking the time of the house to deal with it, because the fruit growers of this area of which I speak are greatly worried today as a result of the condition existing in their industry.
The fruit and vegetable industry of my constituency dates back to the last century. Some of the original orchards were planted
464	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Jones by Lord Aberdeen when he was here representing His Majesty in Canada. This industry is the result of encouragement by the provincial and federal governments all through the years. Not only that; it has progressed remarkably well. It has proved to be a good investment for both those governments, as a source of both direct and indirect taxes for the municipal, provincial and federal coffers. Originally, fruit and vegetables were planted in the interior of British Columbia as a source of food for the settlers in western Canada. Later on, as the industry progressed, at the request and with the encouragement of the government, the producers geared their industry to supply the United Kingdom demand which called for a different size of apple, a different type of apple and an apple of a different colour. The industry therefore for many years has been geared up to meet that demand in what today is a lost market; and that is part of our problem.
For many years now we have been producing fruit of an exceedingly high quality for the markets of the world; and I mean high quality in uniform, dependable grades. This high grade of our fruit and the help of the federal trade commissioners enabled us to compete in nearly every important market of the world. The fruit growers in the British Columbia tree-fruit area are grateful for the financial assistance given to them by the federal government from time to time; but our industry suffered possibly more than did any other industry in Canada during the war and post-war years. That suffering was not as a result of anything of our doing. It was beyond our control. Part of it resulted from currency control, part of it through the economic ills of the importing countries, partly through the difficulties existing in the sterling areas and partly through the United States' subsidies paid on apples to what were formerly markets for British Columbia tree fruit. Today the United States subsidizes apples going to those areas that formerly were our markets to the extent of $1.25 a box or a bushel.
It is true that in times of stress and difficulty some industries can switch quickly from a non-profitable line to a profitable one. But in the fruit industry the fruit producers cannot do that. Theirs is a five to ten-year program, their trees producing when they are from seven to ten years old. They are tied up for a long period with cold storage plants, with irrigation projects, with packing plants, with packing and storage equipment; and you cannot change to any other saleable product using these facilities that are expensive and costly of upkeep. It is just


as silly to suggest that the motor manufacturer who suddenly finds himself unable to sell cars might turn to the making of chocolate biscuits or that the wheat grower on the prairie, suddenly told that there is no more call for wheat, had better grow oranges. It is just as impossible for us in the fruit industry to change overnight to something more profitable.
The federal government has assisted the industry quite substantially since the outbreak of war; that is, from 1939 until today. That assistance amounts to approximately $5 million. But during this period we have produced 90 million boxes of apples. Thus it is seen that the assistance given to the apple producers comes to less than 6 cents a bushel or a box during that time. Opposed to this, however, is the fact that trade agreements consummated between Canada and other countries since 1947 allow oranges, lemons, grapefruit and most imported grapes to be imported into this country duty free. Tariff protection formerly given to our industry has been severely cut. Approximately 60 per cent of our total imports of fresh fruits and vegetables are today admitted duty free. These imports seriously affect the stability of our fruit and vegetable industry.
I should also like to dwell briefly on transportation costs as they affect fruit producers. For a matter of fifty years we in British Columbia have been told that there is a costly part of the railway that has to be paid for by the British Columbia users of that railway through what is called the mountain differential. It has been in varying proportions from double prairie standard rates to one and one-quarter times the prairie standard rates. This practice has gone on for a matter of fifty years. The pretext has been that some bridge existed through the mountains and someone had to bear the cost and pay that loss. Actually there is less than thirty miles of mountain grade on the Canadian Pacific railway in British Columbia-that is on the main line-and there is no mountain grade on the Canadian National railway in British Columbia. The claim has been made of higher construction costs and maintenance. That claim was exploded many years ago. There is no higher construction cost whatever because the materials are better for construction and they are more easily available than in crossing the prairies. We now find that the bridge was not actually in British Columbia at all, but rather in northern Ontario. It took only a matter of weeks for this house to pass a bill to give relief when this bridge was found. Ours had been hidden for fifty years and is yet to be found. In the case of Ontario, they got $7 million a year

to take care of that part of the railway that is considered unprofitable, and I claim that British Columbia should be treated in the same way. As it is, for the last few years we have been penalized in excess rate charges to the amount of between $2 million and $3 million annually. While British Columbia paid this penalty for fifty years, special consideration was given to many other areas of Canada. I will mention a few: The Maritimes Freight Rates Act, the Crowsnest grain rates for the prairies, the feed grain assistance, all of which British Columbia helped directly or indirectly to pay. The royal commission acknowledged these facts and made certain recommendations which I hope will be acted upon.
I believe the railway companies realize that some relief must be given in transportation costs. Otherwise they will kill the apple industry in British Columbia and in the end lose a valuable industry that pays high rates. We do feel the suggestion that has gone forward now that freight rates be equalized as a national policy may help to solve our transportation problem, and we urge the board of transport commissioners to give sympathetic consideration to the case of the British Columbia fruit producers during the hearing on this subject in the very near future.
While our troubles in the industry have caused various communities to seek a balancing influence, several towns have gone out of their way to try to induce new industries to come to settle in the Okanagan valley particularly in order to balance our economy. In January of this year I happened to be attending a growers association conference at Penticton. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) addressed that conference, and lo and behold he strongly advised the growers there represented not to bother with outside industries at all; that the valley was not entirely suitable, but to concentrate on their own fruit and fruit by-products, to develop their own industry based on fruit and vegetables. We have tried that, and we are still trying it. Some years ago we tried to establish a winery in the hope that farmers who grow grapes could find a ready market for them. We have found a fair market for those grapes and wine, but now these people sent me a letter today, part of which I shall quote as follows. It is signed by the president of Calona Wines, Limited:
There is considerable bearing acreage of grapes in British Columbia, and much new acreage coming into bearing each year.
We wish to point out that these growers planted, and are growing these grapes with a view to selling a large percentage of their crops to the wineries of British Columbia.
The Address-Mr. Jones
We would also like to point out that many local people as well as grape growers have invested large sums of money in the wineries of British Columbia, and these wineries are well able to supply the demand for wines in British Columbia.
And incidentally supply other western provinces. I continue:
If American wines are sold in British Columbia-
And that is the question they are faced with today. The letter continues:
If American wines are sold in British Columbia it will mean the British Columbia grape growers and wineries will have a difficult time to stay in business, and as the provincial government is spending thousands of dollars to help build up industries in British Columbia, it is only fair to protect those who have invested their money to build1 British Columbia payrolls.
The grape growers of Ontario have asked for protection against American wines, and our information is that they are being given that protection. As we consider this a serious matter, and immediate action is required-
That immediate action, requested incidentally, is not at all from the federal government because this is a provincial matter. I am just reading the letter to show the house the difficulty facing the industry's by-products division.
The other matter is apple juice. A great deal of apple juice has been processed in the valley, and with a view to extending the market I wrote to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), asking that apple juice be placed on the menu for the army, navy and air force, and I had a very encouraging reply from the minister. But today I received this invitation to tender. It is an invitation to tender for fruit juices and jams. I was rather anxious to find out what success we had in trying to get the navy to purchase apple juice. I find that they are ordering 7,200 tins of fruit cocktail, 7,200 tins of grapefruit juice, 12,800 tins of orange juice. These tins are all 20-ounce tins. Then there are 10,000 tins of pineapple juice, 4,800 tins of blended juice and 1,200 bottles of lime juice, but not an ounce of apple juice. I should like to draw that to the attention of the minister. Possibly he has the best of intentions to see that British Columbia or Ontario apple juice is placed on the menu in the different camps and messes. I hope that by drawing his attention to it, he will have the matter checked, because I think it is unfair to call for these huge quantities of juice that have to be brought into this country from other countries when we have a better product manufactured in our own country.
I am outlining our troubles in the hope that the suggestions I have made will bear fruit. After listening to the minister today giving figures regarding our trade with Great

The Address-Mr. Jones Britain I can see very little hope of increasing what is already an increased figure, but I would suggest that the cabinet consider trying to persuade Great Britain to allow some of the money now being spent in Canada to be diverted to apples. I mention that because we are definitely stuck with apples, grown especially for the United Kingdom market. I do feel that if through the good offices of the cabinet and the ministers concerned, we can induce the British government to sidetrack some of that money they are spending in larger quantities each year towards purchasing our fruit we shall be moving a step forward because I think that would be a good policy. If it were possible for negotiations to be carried out to take payment in sterling or, as I have suggested before, barter for other goods, it would be to our advantage. Foreign markets are a little more difficult. We have sold in practically every country m the world from Egypt to South America and in Japan and China. Through an excellent product we were gaining command of the foreign market until the United States suddenly decided that they were going to try to get into that lucrative market. They have done it not through producing a superior product but through subsidizing the apple industry to the tune of $1.25 a box or $1.25 a bushel. I feel that the whole question of our foreign trade should be referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization, or a special committee should be set up, composed of agricultural members and financial members, to discuss how best we can solve the problems of an industry such as ours in a valley that is geared up_ to a condition that no longer exists. It is a longtime plan that we have to deal with, and I feel that in order to give us help over the present difficulties we should have the government apply a floor price. I m m going to take up the time to deal with that but I make the suggestion to the government that floor prices for apples and vegetables be considered. Again I am suggesting to the cabinet that they instruct the farm loan board to be more generous than they were with the victims of the last severe frost we had in the valley. The conditions under which these farmers can get loans today are more difficult than they were five or even ten years ago because, presumably upon instructions given to farm loan officials on the ground, it appears to be impossible to get decent loans on good risks. I have pointed out before that risks have been turned down by the farm loan board, although they have been acceptable to orthodox loan companies and, in one case, an orthodox bank, for loans of similar amounts.


I feel the intent of the farm loan board should be to be more free with loans than are the banking institutions and the other loan companies. Yet such is not the case. Therefore I would ask the minister to talk this matter over and see if something cannot be done to help these people bridge over this very difficult period in their development.
Owing to the joint calamity of frozen orchards and shrinking markets another problem faces us in the valley, and I refer to the problem of the workers in the industry. The packing house season is very short, and the season for field work is also short, and has also been reduced to a high degree because of difficulties arising from the loss of trees.
The claim period for unemployment insurance has been reduced, as well. This, on top of the seasonal nature of the industry, merits special consideration. I would ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) to survey the conditions now existing in the tree fruit areas where some thousands of men and women are at the moment unemployed. Such a survey should take into consideration unemployment insurance for farm workers. I do believe that if it were extended to farm workers they would be assisted materially in the present crisis.
I would suggest also that the minister consider extending the supplementary claim period until the end of May. As it is today, many of these seasonal workers cannot possibly hope to qualify for unemployment insurance, because of the shorter periods during which they are employed. I feel that in those cases, where men and women have been contributing toward protection they cannot get, and do not hope to get because of the shortness of the season, they should be returned in full any premium they may have paid during the previous year. I believe this would give justice to these people.
I feel also that this survey should take place immediately, and that steps should be taken to try to stabilize the unemployment situation in the tree fruit area. I have here a letter from the city of Kelowna bearing the signature of the city clerk, and endorsing a resolution sponsored by the city of London, in Ontario. While the preamble covers the condition of unemployment in Ontario, the latter part of the letter does cover the situation in British Columbia as well. So, if I may, I should like to read the resolution, which states:
That whereas the dominion government, in the early years of world war II. negotiated with the provinces for the exclusive right to tax income;
And whereas, at the same time, the responsibility for relief of unemployed persons was taken over 100 per cent by the dominion government and the

provinces undertook, on behalf of themselves and their municipalities, to share the cost of maintaining unemployable persons, the ratio of responsibility in Ontario being 50 per cent and 50 per cent;
And whereas over the past twelve years the dominion government has been faced with practically no unemployment problem so that its responsibility for relief of unemployment, in relation to the revenue collected from employers and employees for unemployment insurance premiums, has been negligible, while at the same time the whole burden of relief of unemployable persons has been borne by the provinces and their municipalities;
And whereas the present increase in unemployment due primarily to the dislocation of manufacturing and construction work, as the result of credit restrictions and material priorities, has resulted in numerous appeals to the municipal level of government for assistance, either to eke out inadequate unemployment relief benefits or to substitute for them where the unemployed person is not entitled to benefit or is uncovered by the unemployment insurance regulations;
Therefore be it resolved that the dominion government be requested to take action immediately to survey the unemployment problem and the need for increased unemployment insurance benefits and/or relief assistance, and reduction of the waiting period for collection of unemployment insurance benefit, to the minimum interval possible; that in line with the responsibilities assumed by the dominion in the dominion-provincial conference of 1940, the dominion government forthwith establish, either under dominion, provincial or municipal government supervision, offices for the handling of applications for unemployment relief assistance, so that the intolerable burden will not again be shouldered on to the municipal governments, whose revenues, being restricted almost entirely to real property tax, are not capable of handling this burden, which, under the above mentioned arrangements, was acknowledged as a dominion responsibility in its entirety.
I commend that resolution earnestly, hoping that the government will study it, and take steps to deal with a condition that I knew some time ago was becoming worse, and I now know is acute in the tree fruit area, particularly the Okanagan valley. I would urge the government to take steps immediately to get the facts and information and, if possible, give immediate relief to that hard-pressed industry.

I think they are as fine

men and as sound men as there are in North America. It is not so long ago that Walter Reuther cleaned that element out of the organization. It is not so long ago that his arm was practically blasted off him through a window of his home.

To say that the auto workers union in the United States is controlled by communists is just to indicate to the house that the hon. gentleman had not very much knowledge of the subject that he was talking about. These two men incurred the enmity of all these fellows in the United States to the extent that I have just indicated.
You have to admit that in this country all during the war you did not have any acts of sabotage, you did not have any suggestion of disloyalty in any section of the trade movement; but you found that right here in the government service. That is where the espionage took place, where the trials took place. We could pick them out. But in all the great organizations across this country where there were many opportunities of that kind nothing like that happened. There was not a single case. There was not any evidence of disloyalty on the part of the workers of Canada, and of the trade unions. In that very difficult period they demonstrated their responsibility, their loyalty to the country, both in production and in keeping the organization and the industries free from any subversive elements.
I know the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) would not condone the speech made here today by the hon. member. I read his New Year's message to the workers of Canada, to both congresses, in which he complimented them on their record of production, on their sanity and responsibility, on the contribution they were making to the country, both in industry and socially. He complimented their leaders. My hon. friend, that is the trouble. Your speech was completely contradictory. The hon. member said he believed in trade unions, and yet he characterized their members as hoodlums and as gangsters. He used those words. He was against the high trend in wages. It was all right if it provided a market for farm products. That was a complete contradiction again.
The Address-Mr. Knight
He agreed with unemployment insurance, family allowances, and all of these things that were fought for. Well, you know, they were not got easily. I can remember when there was no unemployment insurance and no family allowance, not even the right to stand in a hall and hold a meeting. My mind goes back to sitting in a little hall and seeing men shot around me by coal company thugs. They were not paying attention to or thinking of social security measures. We had to fight and stick through all that. It is a pattern today; it is accepted today. It is working well, it is working even better than I expected it could work, considering the difficulties we encountered in the early days. All of these measures with which you now agree were fought for by that organized labour movement. I can remember many people in the province I come from who, week after week, month after month, were evicted from their homes and lived in tents during the winter months, with the army and the navy-there was no air force in those days-and with barbed wire all around them. We were struggling for the right to have these things.
I am glad I lived to see things that many of the older people I knew did not live to see. But they had vision. And I am glad to see that we have got around to the point in this country of accepting these things as being necessary in this day and age. I would suggest strongly to the hon. member not to use the propaganda device that was perfected by chambers of commerce a good many years ago to divide the farmers and the workers. We are all working for the same goal. Our interests are identical, and we have to work together.
The attitude he took tonight and the language he used in reference to the trade union movement in my opinion showed poor judgment on his part and provoked me to rise in my place this evening and to say the things I have said.
I am sorry I had to get up and sound off at this time, but I thought that the provocative speech of the hon. member for Vegre-ville and the speech made by my hon. friend across the way required some answer from me, because I am interested personally in both the subjects they raised. I thought their statements were completely in error.

Mr. Speaker,
I had a few words to say before the dinner recess this evening, and indicated that I had something to say in criticism of the Department of National Defence. After listening to the speech of the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Hetland) I decided I would say a word or two about his speech.

The Address-Mr. Knight
Perhaps it is unfortunate that I have to follow my colleague who has just spoken, because I cannot promise to equal either the logic or the wit with which he has kept the house enthralled during the last thirty or forty minutes. Like the hon. member, I deplore the speech of the hon. member for Humboldt.
I took down a few notes of what he said. However I do not think I shall burden the house with a discussion of them, because my colleague has handled the matter well and efficiently. And might I say that when my colleague from Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) sharpens his axe there is no one who is better able to wield it.
I cannot understand the bitter attack against the working people of this country by the hon. member for Humboldt, particularly the attack he made against those in the trade unions. Has not the hon. member, who represents an almost peculiarly rural area in Saskatchewan, and who is a neighbour of mine, any cause affecting the farmers he represents that could have been advanced by him positively in the house, rather than to have taken the negative approach of attacking the urban workers? I wonder if his speech represents the attitude of other Saskatchewan Liberal members toward our fellow men in the towns and cities. I would ask the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Macdonald) and the hon. member for Kootenay East what they think of the statement of their colleague who hails from the rural constituency of Humboldt.
Had the hon. member advanced any arguments, I would have been delighted to have tried to answer them. I cannot do that, however, because no argument was advanced. His whole speech was a masterpiece of selfcontradiction. I do wish to say once again, however, and to say emphatically that, on behalf of the workers in the city of Saskatoon, which I represent, I resent the attack he has made upon the labouring people in this country. May I advise my hon. friend, when he is seeking a subject he understands, and upon which he would be able to speak in the house, not to attempt to speak on labour problems.

I suggest that he ought not to speak about the labouring section of the population, of whom he knows little and with whom he apparently has no sympathy.
Then, before the supper recess I said I would have a word of criticism to offer concerning a transaction of the Department of National Defence. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall follow my notes fairly closely.

because I wish to be sure that what I have to say is documented, and that there are no inaccuracies in it.
To begin with, may I say that I believe I have a serious indictment to bring against the Department of National Defence, an indictment of negligence, carelessness and lack of consideration in its dealings with certain farmers in my constituency in the Dundurn area of Saskatchewan, where there is a military camp.
At some time last summer or last fall-I do not know the dates-the military authorities had mooted the extension of the military camp at Dundurn, and that such extension would involve purchase by the department of the lands of a number of farmers. I have heard the number given as 28, but I am not sure of that.
On January 26 last I was informed of these matters by one of the men involved, notably that he had asked one of the inspectors who had come around to consider the expropriation of these lands if, in fact, he would be likely to have to move oil his place in the fall. This gentleman-and I do not know whether I am describing him correctly when I refer to him as an inspector-told the farmer-and I have the farmer's word for it, as well as the name of the inspector-that he certainly expected the expropriation would take place and that he, the farmer, had better be looking out for another farm.
The farmer proceeded to do just that, namely to look for a suitable farm. He found it, and made a deal. I do not know whether he paid anything on the option on the other farm, but he made a deal pending the decision of the government.
As time went on-and time is of the essence in this particular argument, as you will see later when I develop my theme- he began to get anxious, and asked for a definite decision from the Department of National Defence. He asked whether his land would or would not be expropriated.
He told me that the department-and I have only his word for it-had taken an option. What that means to him, I do not know; but I do know what it means to me. He told me that the department had taken an option on his land. I do not know whether he meant they had paid him anything or not. I should think that would be a legal point.
At any rate, as time went by, realizing the tremendous amount of work involved and the tremendous job it is to move from one farm to another, he wrote to the department asking for a definite decision. And, note this, his letter was not even answered.

Then, more time passed. On January 26- and I have the date in my little notebook- they got in touch with me and asked if I could do anything to find out whether they could then get some money with which they could make a payment so as to make firm this deal for the other farm, or, failing that, whether they could get some definite assurance from the Department of National Defence that their lands would be expropriated. They pointed out that if they had such definite assurance in writing they could go to the bank and borrow sufficient money to make a first payment on the new farm.
As I have said, one of these men complained to me that his letter, written quite some time ago, before he saw me, had not even been answered by the Department of National Defence. Well, I was astonished, because I wish to give the departments credit-not the department in question, but other departments with which I have been in communication-by stating that I have always received prompt answers to my letters, and that they have been most courteous in that regard. But it was not so in this case. I was shocked to learn that the man had written weeks and weeks before and had received no answer. I assured him that I could guarantee to get an answer quickly from the department. On the next day, that is January 27, I wrote a personal letter to the minister. A few days later I had an answer from the executive assistant assuring me that he would make immediate inquiries why the letter had not been answered. When I got that letter from the executive assistant I assumed that he or the minister or somebody in the department would write immediately to the farmer. I thought the matter was closed.
As a matter of fact, I telephoned this man immediately and said, "You are all right, you will be having your answer immediately because I have received word from the executive assistant to the minister." On February 25-I ask you to note that date-four weeks later, my friend telephoned me that he had not yet received a letter from the department. That was the night before I left home. On my arrival in Ottawa I went to the minister's office and gave notice that I intended asking a question next day of the minister. The executive assistant was very sorry about it and said that the file must have been mislaid in the department. He promised to write at once to my constituent, and he did so. I ask you again to note these dates. He wrote two letters, one on March 4 and the other on March 5. The farmer had written quite a while before I had, and my letter was dated January 27.
