Let any one of them get up on his feet now and defend this sort of thing. I am challenging any one of them to do that. I challenge the Minister of National Defence to do it. Let him reply and we will see if we get these sneers from the audience. As I said, I am usually a mild man and I hope that when I do this sort of thing I get credit for doing it with some conviction. I hope it will be given some consideration. This cheap business of not wishing to hear anything that happens to be hurtful to the political side upon which you happen to be is of no credit to you. Let me tell my hon. friends that they are responsible for the administration of this government, and these farmers in the Dundurn area should not be treated like dirt. Just answer that.
I said that the story up to this point had been pretty bad, but from here on it gets worse. Listen to this. On March 4 the minister had said that these options would be taken up. But I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Star-Phoenix, the local newspaper, on March 3. Apparently they had got wind that the farmers had been making certain inquiries and they had telephoned or wired to Ottawa to the Department of National Defence. That is the place where the Minister of National Defence is. That is the same place where the executive assistant is, that is the same place where the head of the department is, that is the place where the orders come from, that is the place where they are supposed to know their business. I said "supposed to" advisedly.
In replying to my question on March 4 the minister said that the options would be taken up. But on March 3 the Star-Phoenix contained a dispatch from Ottawa dated March 1, the day after I had arrived in Ottawa to take up the matter with the government and two days before the minister said that the options were being taken up. As I said, time was an important element in this matter. Perhaps hon. members will believe it now. Perhaps they would like to have another sneer

at this. Try this one on your sneerers and see how you like it. The article reads:
Denies Army Took Land at Dundurn
Ottawa, March 1-Army spokesmen here denied that the defence department had taken over land belonging to 28 farmers near Dundurn to expand the military camp there.
They were commenting on reports that the army had taken over this land but had as yet paid the farmers no money for it. The reports said landowners had made deposits on other land, and that if they did not receive payment from the government soon for their own land, they would lose their deposits on the other land they intended to buy.
The army officials said the Department of Transport, acting as agents for the army, had approached the 28 farmers and had asked them how much money they wanted for their land, in the event of the army taking it over, the spokesman said. Presumably replies had been received from the 28 farmers.
However, these landowners had not been asked to give up their land to the army, nor had any expropriation steps been taken. The inquiries made were purely exploratory and no action had been taken other than to make these inquiries, the spokesmen said.
Whether or not the army actually intended to buy the land in question the officials would not say.
If landowners believed purchase by the army was imminent and had therefore gone out and made a down payment on other property that was "unfortunate" they said. But they claimed that nothing the army nor the transport department had done could lead to such a conclusion.
Then two days later the minister said the options were being taken up. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is the case. Somebody in the Department of National Defence blundered. Has that department no sense, no heart, no head, to leave these people in suspense all that time, with spring getting closer and closer and the people facing the task of moving their households, their machinery, and everything else? They showed an utter disregard for the problems of those people, not even answering their letters of inquiry.
A thought just occurs to me; I ask this question of my hon. friends who I notice have now quit the vocal sneering to which we were subjected a few minutes ago. When would those farmers have been notified if I had not raised the question in the house? Let any one of them answer that question if he wishes. I cannot.
